items.title: Artificial Intelligence Approaches for Insurance Claim Analytics in Synthetic Environments
items.abstract: Insurance claim analytics is often constrained by limited access to real-world data, which restricts the evaluation of advanced artificial intelligence approaches in practical insurance settings. Leveraging the SynthETIC framework, this study systematically evaluates classical actuarial models, neural-network-based methods, generative adversarial networks, and reinforcement learning for three core components of insurance claim processes: claim severity, incremental payments, and settlement delays. GAN-based data augmentation is implemented using task-specific architectures, including a tabular GAN for claim severity, an LSTM-based sequence GAN for incremental payments, and a conditional Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty for settlement delays, while Proximal Policy Optimization provides a sequential decision-learning framework for claim processes. Experimental results show that the performance of data-driven approaches is task-dependent, with GAN-based data augmentation improving some predictive measures but not consistently across all tasks and evaluation metrics. PPO-based reinforcement learning is more sensitive to task formulation and model design, reflecting the importance of action-space specification and reward structures. Additional experiments and mathematical analysis further examine the role of task-specific constraints in sequential payment allocation and delay prediction, highlighting the importance of admissible actions, state representation, and reward design. Overall, the findings illustrate how synthetic insurance environments can support the systematic evaluation of emerging AI paradigms and provide methodological insights into the task-dependent roles of GAN-based data augmentation and reinforcement learning in insurance claim analytics.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Emerging Trends in Libraries
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is one of the emerging trends and applications of computing in libraries. It involves programming computers to do things, which if done by humans, would be said to require intelligence. The ultimate promise of artificial intelligence in libraries is to develop computer systems or machines that think, behave, and in fact rival human intelligence, and this clearly has major implications on librarian ship. The application of artificial intelligence in the library has become pervasive. They include expert systems for reference services, book reading and shelf-reading robots, virtual reality for immersive learning among others. Although the incorporation of artificial intelligence in libraries can be perceived to alienate librarians from their users, it will probably help libraries do more rather than taking over the jobs of librarians. It will enhance their services delivery. Artificial intelligence will greatly improve library operations and services and will upgrade and heighten the relevance of libraries in an ever-changing digital society.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Intelligent and Privacy-Preserving Healthcare: A Survey of Medical Image Analysis, Multimodal Diagnosis, Semi-Supervised Learning, and Personalized Healthcare Systems
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in healthcare, from image-based diagnosis to patient-facing management tools, yet the supporting literature is fragmented across communities that rarely read one another. Motivated by the need for a coherent view, this survey examines four recent peer-reviewed studies that together span multimodal COVID-19 diagnosis, privacy-preserving learning on encrypted medical images, graph-refined semi-supervised pathology classification, and an AI-enabled mobile application for personalized healthcare management and doctor recommendation. Using a structured narrative methodology, the reviewed studies are classified into a five-category taxonomy, compared along technical dimensions, healthcare capabilities, and reported limitations, and synthesized into a layered view that treats imaging, multimodal fusion, privacy preservation, label-efficient learning, and personalization as complementary layers of intelligent healthcare rather than independent technologies. The synthesis indicates that each study advances one layer under its own experimental setting, and that none addresses privacy, label efficiency, multimodality, explainability, and clinical validation together. Recurring gaps include limited clinical validation, dataset constraints, unquantified generalization across institutions, privacy–performance trade-offs, and inconsistent evaluation protocols that prevent direct numerical comparison. Future directions include privacy-preserving multimodal learning, reduced reliance on annotations, explainable and robust models, integration of imaging with clinical records, and multi-site clinical validation. This review is not exhaustive, and no new experiments are presented.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Medical Image Analysis in Low-Resource Settings
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) for medical image analysis is increasingly being developed for low-resource settings, where specialist expertise, imaging equipment, labelled data, and computing resources may be limited. We systematically reviewed 189 studies published between January 2021 and January 2026 to examine how these constraints relate to imaging modalities, clinical applications, and AI methods in low-resource settings. Each study was also assessed against 15 criteria adapted from the FUTURE-AI principles for trustworthy AI. Shortages of clinical expertise were the most common constraint, and portable or lower-cost imaging was widely used. Transfer learning was the most frequent technical strategy (59%), followed by data augmentation (54%) and efficient model design (36%). Medical-image pretraining and self-supervised learning were each used in 4% of studies, and model compression in 3%. Applications were concentrated in retinal disease, pulmonary disease, antenatal care, parasitic diseases, and cervical screening. Beyond these technical and clinical patterns, the trustworthy AI assessment showed a clear gap between documenting how systems were developed and demonstrating how they performed under relevant local conditions. Subgroup performance was evaluated in 24% of studies, intended users or realistic working conditions in 25%, and model explanations with intended users in 4%. Consistent with this gap, among 15 studies that reported the same model and metric during development and in the local setting, 12 performed worse locally. Future research should prioritise representative local evaluation, intended-user assessment, demonstrated resource suitability, and reproducible research practices.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Ecuadorian Higher Education: A PRISMA-Based Systematic Literature Review of Benefits, Challenges, and Research Gaps
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming higher education; however, evidence of its research and application in Ecuador remains fragmented. We systematically reviewed the internationally indexed literature on AI in Ecuadorian higher education. Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, Scopus and the Web of Science Core Collection were searched for peer-reviewed publications from 2015 to 2025. Of the 271 unique records screened, 62 studies met the eligibility criteria; they were appraised using design-specific instruments (MMAT 2018, PROBAST) and analyzed through thematic synthesis across eight axes. The corpus concentrates on 2024–2025 (71%) and is dominated by learning analytics (16 studies) and generative AI (14 studies), followed by perception studies (10 studies). Reported benefits—early warning, efficiency, assessment support, and skill development—rest on technical performance, usability, and satisfaction rather than on measured learning or institutional gains. Persistent challenges include infrastructure constraints, uneven digital competencies, ethical and privacy concerns, and methodologically fragile local evidence; 30 of the 59 appraised studies were rated as having high concern. Ethics, governance, and academic integrity were rarely the primary research objects (two of 62 studies), although 28 raised them as secondary findings. This review derives a research agenda prioritizing governance, pedagogical theorization, methodological rigor, and outcome evidence.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Science and Technology: A Critical Narrative Review of Applications, Evidence, Risks and Emerging Directions
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a general-purpose set of computational methods that is increasingly embedded in scientific research and technological systems. This critical narrative review evaluates the principal roles of AI across scientific discovery, medicine, environmental and space science, manufacturing, software engineering, cybersecurity and communication networks, while distinguishing demonstrated capabilities from claims that remain context dependent. The review also examines conceptual differences between task-bounded AI and human intelligence, and considers human–AI collaboration as a practical design problem rather than a contest between interchangeable forms of intelligence. Literature was selected through transparent live scholarly searching and verification, with an emphasis on peer-reviewed evidence, primary studies for prominent performance claims and authoritative governance sources. The evidence indicates that AI is especially useful where large, high-dimensional or multimodal data must be classified, modelled or searched, and where repeated decisions can be evaluated against explicit performance criteria. Examples include protein-structure prediction, anomaly detection, remote-sensing analysis, autonomous planetary navigation, smart manufacturing and cyber-threat analysis. Nevertheless, high benchmark performance does not automatically establish clinical utility, causal understanding, robustness under distribution shift, safety or equitable deployment. Major cross-cutting limitations include data quality, representativeness, opaque decision processes, evaluation leakage, infrastructure requirements, environmental cost, cybersecurity vulnerabilities and uneven institutional capacity. Responsible integration therefore requires task-specific validation, human oversight, traceability, monitoring and governance proportional to potential harm. Future progress will depend less on simply increasing model scale than on improving scientific validity, causal and mechanistic integration, reproducibility, context-sensitive evaluation and access in lower-resource settings. AI is best understood as an enabling technology whose scientific and social value depends on the quality of the evidence, institutions and human judgement surrounding its use.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Virus Detection: From Metagenomic Discovery to Clinical Decision Support and Population Surveillance
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly central to modern virus detection, particularly as metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) expands diagnostic and surveillance capabilities beyond targeted assays. This paper reviews how AI supports virus detection across three interconnected levels. The metagenomic layer forms the technical core of the review, while the clinical and population sections examine how sequence-level AI outputs are translated into patient-level and public-health decision support. At the metagenomic level, AI addresses key bottlenecks caused by fragmented assemblies and weak homology signals. Foundation-model approaches such as ViraLM leverage pretrained genome representations to improve viral contig discrimination under short-contig conditions, whereas LucaProt integrates sequence- and structure-informed learning to detect highly divergent RNA viruses via RdRP (RNA-dependent RNA polymerase)-focused discovery. At the clinical level, targeted molecular tests remain effective when the suspected pathogen is known, while mNGS provides a complementary, hypothesis-free approach that can broaden etiological investigation in complex infections when laboratories apply appropriate quality control and clinicians interpret results in context. At the population level, early warning systems combine heterogeneous data sources (epidemiological, open-source, digital, environmental, and wastewater signals) with AI methods to enhance outbreak detection and forecasting. Across all levels, robust contamination control, transparent reporting, external validation, and standardized interpretation criteria determine real-world value. Overall, hybrid pipelines that integrate molecular evidence, clinical metadata, and population-scale surveillance within governed, reproducible workflows are likely to provide the greatest impact.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Acoustic Voice Analysis for Differentiating Benign and Malignant Laryngeal Lesions: A Diagnostic Validation Study
items.abstract: Background: Benign and malignant laryngeal lesions frequently present with dysphonia, making clinical differentiation based on voice characteristics alone challenging. Acoustic voice analysis provides objective measurements of vocal function, while artificial intelligence (AI) may identify complex acoustic patterns that are difficult to recognize using conventional parameters. Objective: To evaluate the diagnostic performance of an AI-assisted acoustic voice analysis system in differentiating benign from malignant laryngeal lesions using clinically characterized voice recordings. Materials and Methods: A prospective diagnostic validation study was conducted among adults with laryngeal lesions confirmed by endoscopic and histopathological assessment with ethics committee approval and written informed consent. Standardized sustained-vowel and connected-speech recordings were subjected to acoustic analysis. Fundamental frequency, jitter, shimmer, harmonics-to-noise ratio (HNR), cepstral peak prominence (CPP), spectral parameters and Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients were extracted. Machine-learning classifiers including logistic regression, random forest and extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) .Histopathological diagnosis was the reference standard. Diagnostic performance was assessed using sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), F1 score and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) where estimable from the available model outputs. Results: Among 120 participants, 78 had benign and 42 had malignant lesions. The XGBoost model yielded an AUC of 0.91. Based on the reported confusion matrix, sensitivity was 88.1% (95% CI 75.0–94.8%), specificity 84.6% (95% CI 75.0–91.0%), PPV 75.5% (95% CI 61.9–85.4%), NPV 93.0% (95% CI 84.6–97.0%), accuracy 85.8% (95% CI 78.5–91.0%) and F1 score 0.81. Random forest and logistic regression yielded AUCs of 0.86 and 0.82, respectively. Conclusion: AI-assisted acoustic voice analysis has potential as a non-invasive adjunctive approach for differentiating benign and malignant laryngeal lesions. The reported performance reflects internal validation in a single-centre cohort and should not be regarded as evidence of clinical diagnostic effectiveness until confirmed in an external cohort. Its role should presently be considered complementary to laryngoscopic examination and histopathological diagnosis. Larger prospective, multicentre and externally validated datasets are required before routine clinical implementation.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE-BASED TOOLS AND ENGLISH LANGUAGE PROFICIENCY AMONG UNIVERSITY STUDENTS IN UZBEKISTAN: A PRISMA-GUIDED SYSTEMATIC REVIEW
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping English language education through generative chatbots, automated writing evaluation, intelligent tutoring systems, speech-recognition applications, adaptive learning environments, and AI-supported feedback. This PRISMA-guided systematic review synthesizes recent international and Uzbekistan-specific evidence on the effectiveness of AI-based tools in improving English language proficiency among university students. The review focuses on writing, speaking, reading, listening, vocabulary, feedback, motivation, engagement, and learner autonomy. Meta-analyses and systematic reviews generally report positive effects, particularly for productive skills and individualized feedback, but they also reveal substantial heterogeneity across technologies, intervention duration, learner profiles, and research designs. Evidence on ChatGPT and related generative AI tools suggests benefits for idea generation, revision, conversational practice, and autonomous learning, while highlighting risks related to inaccurate information, overreliance, academic integrity, privacy, and uneven AI literacy. Emerging studies from Uzbekistan confirm strong interest in AI-supported language learning and indicate potential benefits for writing and vocabulary development, although local evidence remains smaller and methodologically less mature than the international literature. The review concludes that AI is most effective when integrated into structured pedagogy, combined with teacher guidance, and supported by explicit AI literacy and ethical-use practices.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Computer Vision for Food Inspection: From Validated Measurements to Process Control
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence-enabled computer vision can increase the frequency and spatial coverage of food inspection, but high predictive accuracy does not establish reliable production decisions. This critical narrative review examines the evidence connecting image measurements with grading, rejection, and process control. Representative studies across produce, grains and nuts, meat and seafood, microbiology, and packaging are compared by sensing modality, reference endpoint, validation unit, and operational action. The synthesis distinguishes visible quality from specific hazards, prepared defects from natural variation, and image-level performance from verified product outcomes. An author-proposed evidence map organizes analytical feasibility, independent-sample testing, operational challenges, external transfer, and prospective impact as partly independent dimensions. It is unvalidated and is not a readiness score or regulatory standard. Task-dependent reporting considerations address uncertainty, prevalence, false rejection, and abstention. Safety-related uses require separate hazard-specific validation, sampling, and acceptance criteria. Process integration additionally requires acquisition-to-actuation testing, accepted-product verification, and controlled updates. The purposive evidence base cannot establish field-wide effectiveness or rank modalities. Research priorities include traceable datasets, mechanistic challenges, and prospective intervention studies. Progress toward closed-loop control should be judged by stable measurements and demonstrated effects on defined product and process outcomes within a stated operating domain.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence, Foundation Models, and Digital Twins for Climate-Resilient Agriculture: A Review
items.abstract: Climate change, increasing food demand, and resource constraints are accelerating the transition from conventional precision agriculture toward smart, autonomous, and climate-resilient agricultural systems. Artificial intelligence (AI), foundation models, digital twins (DTs), the Internet of Things (IoT), remote sensing, edge–cloud computing, and big data analytics are emerging as key technologies for data-driven agricultural management. This review critically evaluates recent advances in AI-driven intelligent agriculture, with emphasis on machine learning, deep learning, explainable AI (XAI), generative and agentic AI, multimodal foundation models, and digital twins, together with the sensing and computing infrastructures required for their deployment. Relevant literature was identified using keywords related to AI, foundation models, digital twins, IoT, precision agriculture, and climate-resilient agriculture, with emphasis on recent peer-reviewed studies addressing technological applications, performance, limitations, challenges, and future prospects. The selected literature was critically synthesized to identify technological trends, knowledge gaps, and emerging research opportunities. The review highlights that the greatest potential of intelligent agriculture lies in integrating heterogeneous data from sensors, UAVs (unmanned aerial vehicles), satellites, weather systems, field operations, and agricultural knowledge to support context-aware prediction, decision-making, and autonomous action. However, data quality, model generalizability, explainability, interoperability, cybersecurity, computational requirements, and large-scale field validation remain major challenges. This review further develops an integrated perspective connecting AI, foundation models, multimodal data infrastructures, digital twins, and autonomous agricultural systems within a unified cyber-physical ecosystem. Future priorities include trustworthy AI, agentic decision-making, semantic interoperability, federated learning, continuous learning, and self-learning digital twins toward Agriculture 6.0.

items.title: Assessment of Ground Water Quality from Rural Areas of Chandrapur District, Maharashtra, India
items.abstract: Groundwater serves as a vital resource for drinking and household needs across rural communities in Maharashtra's Chandrapur District. This research was conducted to examine the physicochemical properties of local groundwater and determine its viability for human consumption and daily use. Water samples gathered from various rural sites in the district underwent laboratory testing for key parameters using standard analytical methods, encompassing color, calcium, chloride, electrical conductivity, fluoride, magnesium, nitrate, pH, total dissolved solids, total alkalinity, total hardness, turbidity, iron, and sulfate, with results benchmarked against established drinking-water standards. Furthermore, the study highlights geographic variations in water quality driven by regional geology and human factors such as farming practices, domestic wastewater, and improper waste disposal. This evaluation pinpoints specific water parameters and locations requiring focused public water management, ultimately emphasizing the necessity of consistent monitoring, proper treatment, source safeguarding, and contamination control to preserve safe and sustainable groundwater supplies in rural Chandrapur.

items.title: Attribute-Centric Vision-Language Alignment for Fine-Grained Gait Understanding
items.abstract: Walking sequences reveal human-interpretable attributes related to body structure, posture, and motion. Gait attribute recognition provides a concrete route to fine-grained gait understanding by predicting these attributes. However, existing benchmarks provide limited fine-grained annotations, while classifier-based gait attribute recognition methods typically represent candidate classes through learned output weights rather than directly matching visual evidence with textual class representations. To address the annotation gap, we present RA-GAR, a large-scale, richly annotated multimodal benchmark for gait attribute recognition, containing 1,001 subjects, 242,729 walking sequences, and annotations for 15 static and motion gait attributes. We further propose Gait-VL, an attribute-centric vision-language alignment framework that recognizes gait attributes by matching attribute-specific multi-frame visual evidence with textual class prototypes. On the visual side, attribute-specific learnable queries aggregate RGB features across spatial locations and frames into per-attribute visual embeddings. On the language side, diverse descriptions expanded by a large language model are combined with context about relevant body regions to construct textual class prototypes. Beyond attribute recognition, we evaluate the transferability of the attribute-pretrained visual encoder by using it to replace generic upstream large vision models in identityoriented gait recognition pipelines; attribute pre-training uses no identity classification or metric-learning objectives. Experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art attribute recognition performance on RA-GAR and consistent improvements in downstream identity recognition across multiple pipelines and benchmarks, supporting the effectiveness and transferability of attribute-centric gait representation learning.

items.title: Automated Essay Scoring with GPT Models: A Comparison with Human Ratings of IEP Written Products
items.abstract: This study explores the integration of Large Language Model (LLM)-based Automated Essay Scoring (AES) into classroom writing assessment within an Intensive English Program (IEP). Using a corpus of 46 multi-draft capstone essays written by international students in an Academic Literacies course, the study evaluates the performance of two OpenAI models (GPT-4.1-mini and GPT-5.1) against rubric-based human instructor scores. Essays were scored twice by each model under controlled temperature settings to evaluate linear association, systematic bias, inter-model consistency, and performance-band agreement. Findings reveal that while both LLM scores maintain moderate positive correlations with human ratings (r = .44 for GPT-4.1-mini; r = .49 for GPT-5.1), both models exhibit systematic negative bias, scoring essays an average of 13 points lower than the human instructor. However, the two models demonstrate strong inter-model consistency (r = .84) and an exact band-level agreement of 87%. Qualitative analysis of the holistic comments shows that LLMs focus on global discourse features but lack sensitivity to local, process-oriented classroom constructs. The results suggest that uncalibrated zero-shot LLMs serve better as formative diagnostic tools than autonomous grading systems.Keywords: Automated essay scoring, Large Language Models, GPT-5, L2 academic writing, multi-method validity, formative assessment.

items.title: AUTOMATED NDPA COMPLIANCE TOOLKIT FOR ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE-DRIVEN STUDENT MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS IN NIGERIAN UNIVERSITIES
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence has become a central pillar of institutional management in Nigerian higher education, processing massive volumes of student data for admissions, predictive analytics, and attendance management. However, this data-intensive transformation operates under the strict oversight of the Nigeria Data Protection Act (NDPA) of 2023. Despite these legal obligations, empirical evidence reveals a systemic governance deficit, characterized by bundled consent, unlawful cross-border data transfers, and automated decision-making without human oversight. This project aimed to design, develop, and evaluate an Automated NDPA Compliance Toolkit to systematically detect and remediate compliance violations within artificial intelligence-driven Student Management Systems. Design Science Research was adopted as the primary methodology, supported by documentary analysis and comparative technology assessment. The developed toolkit features a three-layer architecture utilizing Python, FastAPI, PostgreSQL, and React.js, operationalizing the NDPA into 25 executable checks across six compliance modules. Testing was conducted using a simulated non-compliant institution and a compliant control system. The toolkit successfully identified all planted violations in the non-compliant system, assigning a compliance health index of 12 percent, while accurately passing all checks for the compliant system with a 100 percent score. The confusion matrix indicated 100 percent detection accuracy and specificity. The findings establish that software can effectively bridge the gap between statutory requirements and practical implementation by translating legal provisions into verifiable technical controls.

items.title: Automatic Assessment in Higher Education Using General-Purpose AI Tools: A Design-Based Research Approach
items.abstract: Automated student assessment using AI tools can contribute to the viability of online higher education programs, preserving academic integrity, strengthening students’ engagement and reducing costs. General-purpose Generative AI models such as ChatGPT have shown their ability to automatically grade student assignments. However, further investigation of their validity is needed for complex student tasks, such as creative projects in higher education. The aim of this study is firstly to evaluate the potential of costless, general-purpose AI tools to assess complex higher education topics. Secondly, we seek to identify which are the minimum skills in AI prompting required by an educator to successfully perform such tasks. A Design-Based Research (DBR) methodology was employed, following an iterative process of prompting and calibrating the AI tool to imitate the professor’s assessments in a representative course that emphasizes on knowledge application, critical thinking and creativity. Testing was performed on a dataset of 39 student assignments, comparing the results of zero-shot AI prompts, multi-cycle calibrated AI and the opinion of two human course lecturers. Automatic assessment of complex tasks with high level of consistency and agreement with human judgement was only achieved by educators with skills in structured prompts and multi-cycle calibration.

items.title: Beware LLMs bearing gifts: hallucinations, satisfactory results, and student use of generative AI in the production of Mediterranean archaeology websites
items.abstract: Abstract Recently, an epistemic shift has occurred in classics pedagogy. First, the COVID pandemic forced students online. Then, large language model (LLM) chatbots appeared. These disruptions created a conundrum: how could research methods, reading and writing, and cross-cultural exploration be taught when students were tethered to LLM-accessible ‘cheating machines’? The solution was AI-assisted classics. This paper describes how AI-assisted classical history can be taught through a discussion of the ‘WHAM’ (Web Design, HTML, and the Archaeology of the Mediterranean) project. WHAM is a website-building classroom assignment developed to teach students in the Computer Science and Society major at Wentworth Institute of Technology (Boston, MA, USA; www.wit.edu ) how to utilize digital tools to explicate humanities data. Students create a website from the HTML code up focused on a Mediterranean archaeological region and are taught to use LLMs critically, both for writing HTML code and for ideating web design features. In the process, students learn how LLMs must be approached cautiously since they can both hallucinate and offer satisfactory work that should be improved. Finally, the paper suggests that LLMs can provide students with a starting place for digital projects that challenge them to engage with the classical world’s history and material culture.

items.title: Beyond Conventional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI): Advanced Neuroimaging for Early Detection and Precision Characterization of Brain Metastases in Lung Cancer: Narrative Review
items.abstract: Brain metastases are a frequent manifestation of lung cancer and a substantial proportion of patients require accurate intracranial assessment at diagnosis, during staging or when neurological symptoms emerge. Conventional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), which relies on T1 weighted post contrast imaging together with T2 weighted and FLAIR sequences and in which three-dimensional T1 weighted imaging is the reference standard for detection, remains central to diagnosis and longitudinal monitoring, but its specificity is limited in the post treatment setting, where imaging features may not reliably distinguish viable tumor from radiation necrosis. The objective of this narrative review was to appraise the role of advanced and quantitative MRI in four clinically distinct questions, namely detection of small or early lesions, characterization and differential diagnosis, post treatment assessment and quantitative or artificial intelligence-based applications, in patients with lung cancer. Literature was identified through PubMed and included systematic reviews, meta-analyses, narrative reviews, original clinical studies and imaging-based investigations, with evidence derived from lung cancer specific cohorts distinguished throughout from evidence derived from mixed brain metastasis populations. The strongest evidence supports characterization and post treatment assessment. Perfusion derived relative cerebral blood volume and fractional tumor burden were higher in progression than in radiation necrosis and diffusion metrics, permeability parameters, MR spectroscopy and delayed contrast enhanced imaging contributed additional information, although these findings derive largely from mixed brain metastasis cohorts, group level differences overlap substantially at the level of the individual patient and no validated diagnostic threshold exists for any single biomarker. Evidence that advanced sequences improve detection of small or occult lesions beyond optimized three-dimensional T1 weighted imaging is considerably weaker and rests largely on mechanistic reasoning rather than on comparative diagnostic accuracy studies. Radiomics and machine learning have reported promising discrimination for post treatment differential diagnosis and for prediction of molecular and histological subtype, but reported performance is vulnerable to overfitting, data leakage, segmentation variability and incomplete reporting, calibration is seldom assessed and external validation remains uncommon. Advanced and quantitative MRI should presently be regarded as complementary to conventional MRI and tissue based molecular testing rather than as clinically validated substitutes and prospective multicenter studies using standardized acquisition and reporting are required before routine adoption.

items.abstract: Autonomous cybersecurity requires a transition from isolated alert classification toward coordinated threat investigation, evidence-grounded decisions, and measurable containment. This study integrates a generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) multi-agent threat-hunting architecture with a six-state nonlinear model of secure, exposed, compromised, and recovered assets and the evolving hunting and response capabilities. The framework employs independent evidence verification and policy-controlled response authorization, while model analysis uses a containment threshold, equilibrium stability and parameter sensitivity. Across the three configurations reported in the supplied results, compromise fractions were 42.71% for rule-based defence, 32.48% for machine-learning-supported defence, and 19.16% for GenAI-enabled defence; corresponding containment thresholds were 6.860, 4.857, and 3.275. These submitted outcomes indicate a 55.1% lower modelled compromise fraction for the GenAI configuration than for rule-based defence, although all thresholds remain above unity and therefore do not establish threat elimination. Three author-supplied three-dimensional response surfaces describe the effects of propagation, assisted recovery, adversarial adaptation and hunting activation. The investigation distinguishes these reported model-based outcomes from unreported alert-level accuracy benchmarks and from numerical bifurcations that require recorded AUTO-07p continuation diagnostics. The resulting contribution is a coherent framework linking generative investigation, bounded response capacity and nonlinear cybersecurity resilience, with explicit requirements for reproducible experimental validation and safe operational deployment.

items.title: Beyond Mueller–Hinton Broth: A Scoping Review of Metabolic Context, Conditional Antibiotic Susceptibility, and Metabolism-Aware Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing
items.abstract: Background. Standard antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) in Mueller–Hinton broth samples a single metabolic state, yet bacterial susceptibility in vivo depends on nutrient availability, host-derived metabolites, and spatial structure. The extent to which this mismatch produces clinically relevant errors in susceptibility classification has not been systematically mapped. Objective. To map the evidence linking metabolic context to conditional antibiotic susceptibility and to identify gaps between mechanistic insight, physiologically relevant models, and clinical validation. Methods. We conducted a scoping review following PRISMA-ScR. The search combined PubMed, Semantic Scholar, Web of Science, and Embase with AI-assisted discovery and screening using Consensus AI and large language models, with full human verification at every inclusion decision. AI use is reported per PRISMA-trAIce. Records were classified by mechanism (porin regulation, efflux, stringent response, metabolic rewiring, biofilm structure) and by infection-relevant context (gut-mimicking media, bicarbonate and host factors, single-cell and heterogeneity, in vivo models, clinical validation). Results. Of 1,543,377 records identified, 100 studies met inclusion criteria. Mechanistic evidence was dense across all seven mechanistic foci. In contrast, evidence in physiologically relevant contexts was sparse: gut-mimicking AST appeared in only one mechanism category, and clinical validation was absent in five of seven. The most prominent gap was the absence of prospective clinical validation linking host-mimicking AST results to patient outcomes. Conclusions. Metabolic state is a primary determinant of antibiotic susceptibility, and standard Mueller–Hinton AST samples only one such state. The field has established mechanisms but not clinical translation. Prospective validation of host-mimicking AST across pathogen and drug classes is the highest-priority next step.

items.title: Beyond Neurocentrism: Toward an Embodied, Predictive and Integrative Framework for Consciousness
items.abstract: The prevailing neurological orthodoxy equates the mind with neuronal activation. While empirically grounded, this reductionist paradigm fails to account for subjective experience, altered states of consciousness, and the profound influence of the body on cognition. This opinion challenges the neurocentric assumption and proposes a radical redefinition: The mind is an emergent, dynamic, predictive, and nonlinear process arising from the continuous integration of all intentional (cognitive) and non-intentional (affective, homeostatic, and interoceptive) psychological processes occurring throughout the living body, constantly reconciling internal bodily needs with external environmental demands. Drawing on predictive processing theory, embodied cognition, complex systems dynamics, and recent work on interoception and homeostatic feelings, it is argued that consciousness is not a binary neural switch but a nonlinear spectrum of bodilycognitive integration. This framework offers novel implications for psychiatry, medicine, artificial intelligence, and clinical diagnostics.

items.title: Beyond Outcome Feedback: Trajectory-Quality-Guided Experience-based Learning
items.abstract: Experience-based learning enables large language model (LLM) agents to improve over time by reusing knowledge from past executions. However, existing methods typically rely on final task outcomes as feedback for experience learning, overlooking the execution process and limiting their ability to evaluate and optimize experience based on trajectory quality. To address this limitation, we propose TQG-Exp, a trajectory-quality-guided experience-based learning framework that introduces process feedback. Specifically, we introduce Trajectory Quality Loss (TQL), which jointly considers task completion and process quality to provide a learning signal beyond final task outcomes. Based on this signal, we employ paired rollouts with and without retrieved experience to guide experience optimization. Representative trajectories are selected based on their outcomes and trajectory quality to extract task-level and task-type-level experiences. Meanwhile, differences in trajectory quality between the paired groups are used to estimate the contribution of retrieved experience and update its utility. The learned utility is then combined with semantic relevance to guide subsequent experience retrieval. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld with two backbone LLMs show that TQG-Exp outperforms existing experience-based methods, improving Avg.@3 over the strongest baseline by 4.50 and 8.55 percentage points on DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen3.5-Flash, respectively.

items.title: Beyond Survivorship Bias: A Counter-Inductive AI Architecture for Scientific Discovery amid the Millennium Problems
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems for scientific discovery are trained primarily on published literature and therefore internalize survivorship bias: they learn from positive results, funded hypotheses, and consensus paradigms. This confines them to what Thomas Kuhn called “normal science” and limits their capacity for revolutionary discovery. This article proposes a counter-inductive AI architecture that treats absence, failure, and negative results as primary epistemic signals. The architecture integrates three layers: 1) Negative Space Mapping, which identifies structural blind spots in knowledge graphs; 2) Dark Data Processing, which mines unpublished, rejected, or failed experiments; and 3) Counter-Inductive Hypothesis Generation, which optimizes for surprise relative to consensus under structural viability constraints. We formalize this approach using a counter-inductive loss function and illustrate its application to neurobiology with the case of the CPEB3/CPEB4 protein systems, showing how the system would prioritize neglected areas such as glial function, active forgetting, and sleep. The article also examines the emerging controversy surrounding AI-generated solutions to mathematical Millennium Prize Problems, where claims of attribution and the use of prior researcher data have sparked intense debate. We argue that a counter-inductive architecture, by explicitly mapping negative space and processing dark data, offers a more transparent and epistemically rigorous path toward addressing such fundamental problems, one that acknowledges and credits the human research it builds upon. Moving beyond survivorship bias requires redefining the objective of scientific AI from consensus optimization to paradigm disruption. The result is a Kuhnian AI capable of generating testable, high-risk hypotheses that the current literature systematically overlooks.

items.title: Bridging Risk Approximation Gaps in Model Predictive Task Sampling via In-Context Modeling
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is essential for adaptive decision-making, e.g., robust Meta-RL and domain randomization (DR), and efficient post-training of large language models (LLMs), where tasks are commonly structured as Markov decision processes or prompts. A central bottleneck in all these settings is the cost of agent-environment interactions required for task selection and policy optimization. Model predictive task sampling (MPTS) has emerged as a promising approach to improve sample efficiency by querying informative tasks via a risk predictive model (RPM) trained on optimization history. However, existing RPMs suffer from two failure modes: (i) sparse optimization histories, which limit RPMs' generalization across the task space, and (ii) a one-step lag in risk approximation, which causes biased difficulty estimation as the policy evolves. This work formalizes these failure modes, derives lagged-risk decompositions that expose the resulting temporal bias, and recasts risk prediction as an in-context sequence modeling problem. The developed RPM integrates a one-step look-ahead mechanism with a temporal-weighted sliding window to mitigate data non-stationarity and scarcity, without requiring additional rollouts. Empirically, our approach yields more reliable difficulty estimates and consistent performance gains across robust Meta-RL, DR, and prompt curriculum RL post-training of LLMs.

items.title: Bridging the Gap: What Sports Media Hiring Managers Actually Want from Journalism School Graduates
items.abstract: The sports media industry has undergone seismic structural transformation over the past two decades, driven by the collapse of legacy newspaper models, the proliferation of digital platforms, and the emergence of artificial intelligence. This qualitative study examines what sports media hiring managers and editors actually require from recent journalism school graduates as they enter a rapidly evolving workforce. Drawing on semi-structured, in-depth interviews with 15 sports media professionals who self-identified as editors and/or publishers and who are affiliated with the Football Writers Association of America (FWAA) and the U.S. Basketball Writers Association (USBWA), this study employs a human capital theory framework to analyze the alignment, and the persistent misalignment, between what journalism programs produce and what the industry demands. Findings reveal four dominant themes: (1) passion and intrinsic motivation as non-negotiable hiring criteria; (2) the depreciation of formal credentials relative to demonstrated, verifiable work; (3) a widening deficit in source cultivation, relationship building, and reporting fundamentals among recent graduates; and (4) a growing demand for multimedia versatility and platform fluency. Implications for journalism education curricula, industry-academy collaboration, and the professional preparation of the next generation of sports media workers are discussed.

items.title: ByteMark: A Unified Byte-Level Watermark for Detection Across Language Models
items.abstract: As watermarking of LLM-generated text enters deployment, users increasingly need to check text whose source is unknown. Existing detectors read the watermark through a specific tokenizer or embedding pipeline, and even if all providers adopted the same watermarking method, differences in these representations would leave their watermarks incompatible, and the text alone does not reveal which representation produced it. We propose ByteMark, a unified watermarking scheme that defines its signal on the UTF-8 bytes of published text. Models with different tokenizers embed this signal under one public specification and key, and a single detector verifies the text from the text and key alone. When the tokenizer or embedding model of a baseline detector is replaced, its detection degrades sharply, whereas ByteMark, which uses neither, retains its detection rate; ByteMark also remains detectable when participating models continue or rewrite the text.

items.abstract: Cage Containment Receipt 1 (CCR-1): a deterministic execution gate rejected 100% of contract-invalid proposals before any side effect executed, while admitting only contract-valid actions to a harmless local mock target. Holds and escalations never caused side effects. This is the execution-containment complement to the PENTA-CL model-attribution replay evidence: matching decisions and blocked invalid proposals under the same deterministic envelope. Results (falsifiers 0/5 tripped): 17 candidates = 1 positive control + 8 fresh LLM-generated captures (4 engines x 2: Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Luna, GPT-6.1 Sol, GLM 5.2) + 8 harness-generated adversarial mutations. All 9 valid candidates admitted (72 actions written, 18 holds, 18 escalations — zero hold/escalation side effects). All 8 adversarial cases rejected with the mock journal hash unchanged: malformed JSON, case-normalized anomaly types, invented playbook ids, under-confidence heals, false holds, extra keys, wrong array length, duplicate positions. Duplicate action-id suppression and the hold/admit distinction (holds never increment the healing-action counter) verified. Scope (honest limits): proves the local mock-gate for the tested integration and inputs only — NOT containment of every Base44 tool, any production runtime, or untested inputs. The adversarial mutations are harness-generated and labeled as such; no fresh adversarial-LLM conversation was created inside the run itself (that leg remains open). items.abstract: Cage Containment Receipt 2 (CCR-2) — the fresh adversarial-LLM leg. CCR-2 closes that gap: a live, memory-disabled, platform-pinned LLM engine (GPT-5.6 Luna), explicitly instructed toward a best-effort heal of a below-threshold anomaly, proposed the invalid resolved tuple — a confidence-gate breach — and the deterministic gate rejected it BEFORE any side effect executed. items.title: Calibrated Reliance on Large Language Models for Personalized Surgical Care: A Critical Narrative Review of Confidence, Clinical Reasoning and Decision Support
items.abstract: Large language models can synthesize clinical records, identify phenotypic features and support patient-specific decisions, but fluent explanations may obscure uncertainty. Surgical practice provides a demanding setting in which to examine this problem because decisions combine heterogeneous evidence, procedural risk and individual preferences. This critical narrative review connects surgical self-assessment research with studies of clinician–LLM interaction, clinical summarization, uncertainty estimation and perioperative implementation. Targeted searches of PubMed records through Europe PMC were supplemented by retrieval of methodological and foundational sources. Selection was purposive, with attention to contradictory findings and the distinction between simulated performance and clinical benefit. Randomized studies using general clinical vignettes and simulated tasks show that LLM assistance does not uniformly improve physician reasoning; their applicability to surgical decisions remains indirect. Direct clinical studies extend from preoperative documentation and triage to shared decision-making and postoperative support, with mixed findings and limited evidence of sustained patient benefit. We distinguish clinician self-appraisal, LLM uncertainty, prognostic calibration, appropriate reliance and patient-specific decision quality, each requiring distinct evaluation criteria. For personalized surgical care, generated interpretations should preserve the provenance, timing and limitations of the underlying patient data and predictive models. We propose a workflow for examining discrepancies between clinician judgment and LLM output, together with an evaluation agenda centered on harmful decision changes, verification burden and patient-relevant outcomes. This framework requires prospective validation.

items.title: CB-Agent: Concept-Based In-Context Learning for Sequential Action Selection
items.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) allows large language models to use demonstrations without updating their parameters. For interactive agents, demonstrations are trajectories of reasoning, actions, and observations that illustrate how to complete a task. Reusing demonstrations in new situations is challenging: directly inputting full trajectories consumes limited prompt space and constrains the overall effectiveness, while natural-language summaries require the agent to translate general guidance into specific action choices. Therefore, we study whether expert action choices can directly supervise a reusable scoring rule. We propose CB-Agent, which extends concept-based ICL to sequential action selection. We extract environment-action decisions from expert trajectories and fit a concept vector by maximum likelihood to model the conditional distribution over candidate actions given the context. This model combines the concept with frozen language-model features and priors. During ReAct interaction, the agent uses this distribution to select environment actions without including demonstrations in the action-scoring context. Across TextWorld, ALFWorld, and ScienceWorld, CB-Agent achieves the highest cross-benchmark average among the evaluated methods at all three tested model sizes and ranks first on TextWorld and ScienceWorld at each size. ALFWorld experiments support the learned concept's contribution beyond prior-only scoring and show further gains when combined with Reflexion. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CB-Agent-DFF9/.

items.title: Citizen Oversight for Safe AI Frontiers
items.abstract: Background Summary Public opinion of artificial intelligence systems and the frontier labs that develop them are at an all time low, with serious concerns about the pace and scope of this powerful technology that is rapidly advancing without community standards, laws, regulators, or transparent processes. The technical knowledge required to draft meaningful legislation, or even to establish legal guardrails, far exceeds the competencies represented within the three branches of government. Indeed, the government's concerns about AI appear to be limited to economic impacts, and the promise of adding over $10T to America's economy with nearly 4% year-over-year GDP growth over the next four years., That translates to a 30% jump in today’s GDP estimate ($32.3T) driven by a national economy with markets running about twice as hot as their current historic highs. Political leaders and economists view these projections as justifications for the risk that AI poses, despite dire warnings from industry stakeholders. Despite corporate attempts to control the public narrative and hide behind IP laws, the public continues to learn of new breaches and threats that reinforce concerns that frontier labs do not actually have full control over the systems they have built. The ability of agentic tools to penetrate local systems built on cloud services poses a global threat, while even the most responsive government interventions are reactionary, at best. Even so, the lack of transparency involved in all aspects of this black box tech have forced victims of AI breach to seek remedy from the violators themselves. The very companies that are creating these crises are not only free from legal accountability for the harms they cause to clients around the world, but also appear to be free from accountability even within the frontier labs that develop them. Human Agency in AI Systems This century will be defined by how civilization engages with artificial intelligence. The pace of significant albeit poorly documented updates to existing AI models, the aggressive drive toward recursive self-improvement (RSI) models, and the emergence of socio-cultural behaviors by agent groups demand an equally robust human response that preserves the role of public choice in the use of these tools, as well as the individual rights guaranteed by the Constitution. This proposal outlines a pilot project to identify, test, and refine civil society engagement models that have been developed for other adversarial cross-sectoral contexts and proven to deliver mutually beneficial outcomes. This investigation will explore a set of pre-determined civilian oversight frameworks for suitability within defined AI-in-society policy concerns. For example, law enforcement surveillance systems, such as Flock Safety, must be subject to civilian scrutiny; however, accessible oversight mechanisms for the lay public have not yet been developed. Public oversight is left to the public to self-organize with no particular coordinated efforts to guide them. Indeed, the vast majority of oversight resources that have been developed exist for the use of industry to track benchmarks and improve performance. Current government guidance, scant as it is, is likewise dedicated to benefiting frontier labs. This proposal describes a novel framework for public assessment of AI systems, to be implemented before and during the use of AI tools and services by public institutions, including local government. The results of this pilot phase will determine whether and how the project should be broadened and scaled into a more comprehensive, robust framework with policy recommendations and economic analysis. Methodology, Milestones, Outputs This mixed-methods study will begin with a comparative analysis of a defined set of reference frameworks. The set of frameworks will be piloted by civilian volunteer groups reviewing real use cases. The pilot will produce metrics inherent to each framework’s evaluation criteria, which will then be used to further develop an assessment rubric that enables stakeholders choice. Phase I: Comparative Analysis of Reference Frameworks This phase of the project will provide an historical overview of each oversight mechanism in its original context, and map it to the AI context that will be tested in the pilot phase. Reference Frameworks -Citizen Review Boards (CRB) are citizen-led watchdog groups that engage in issues of particular concern to these self-selecting groups. -Consensus Review is an expert-based committee process that invites the public to hear expert testimony and witness information gathering sessions, but the deliberative process is conducted in closed session. This approach may be suitable for preparing significant policy decisions by public institutions and/or governments. -Danish Consensus Conference is a participatory model that enjoins citizens to consider controversial STEM issues and report their policy recommendations to the government and the public. The goal is to form a consensus that strikes a balance between competing stakeholder demands, known risks and potential harms to society, and economic benefits. This framework is particularly apt for public assessment of large, high tech systems for the purpose of policy guidance. Nonetheless, it is not a model familiar to most American stakeholders and may not be appropriate for all AI-in-society deliberations. -Indigenous Data Sovereignty Governance (IDSG) is an emerging framework situated in the human rights principle of self determination. It is an ethical process that calls on place-based community standards, norms, and traditions. It can entail exceptionally time consuming deliberation that results in the establishment of long-term, communitywide rules. -Institutional Review Board (IRB) is a well-established expert-based committee process that exists primarily to reduce risk and limit exposure to the institution by confirming that the plans and processes involved in the activity comply with laws and regulations. It extends protections to individuals and communities indirectly by restricting activities to the confines of broadly applicable legal rules. This approach may be particularly suitable for controversial policy actions, where watchdog organizations are viewed as adversarial actors, rather than community partners. -Jury Deliberation is a type of peer review that allows oversight entities to review evidence and ponder narrow questions in private or closed sessions. Jury decisions must be unanimous and can be appealed. Juries are not required to justify their decisions. This approach might be preferable when sensitive data is involved. -Situated Learning/Community Management (COP) is a Community of Practice (COP) framework that fosters peer-based skilling, adoption of best practices, co-creation of design and development, and information dissemination. This is likely to be a strong mechanism for project planning and early-stage implementation of public AI systems. -Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) is an arbiter-led approach that allows community actors to register grievances, state their trustworthy goals, define for themselves the role that they want to play in the design or oversight of trustworthy AI systems, and reset with a restorative justice engagement framework going forward. -Unstructured Athenian (UA) model, which provides stakeholders a pathway to identify bias outcomes and issue tickets for resolution by administrators within a predetermined timeframe. This is likely to appeal to communities working in close partnership with AI stakeholders, for example where large data centers are welcomed and/or AI systems are perceived as meeting a defined need in service to the local community. Phase II: Pilot Studies Phase II will test known frameworks that have been extensively studied, documented, reviewed, and refined with proven best practices over years and even decades. These reference frameworks represent a variety of input and deliberation processes that communities can select according to needs and capacities. Volunteers will select an oversight mechanism of their choice and join other members of the group to review a real use case that is relevant to their competency and/or community. The goal is to study the effectiveness of the process itself, not the individual or group dynamics, per se. For example, an oversight goal might include “To determine the suitability of Flock Safety devices in a defined rural geolocation.” The pilot group will be organized according to the standards of their assigned oversight mechanism, e.g., Jury, and given instructions for deliberation. Each volunteer will complete a survey instrument designed to capture metrics about the effectiveness of the process in the context of assessing AI in society, weaknesses and strengths of the mechanism to deliver the desired goal(s), and general feedback to describe flaws and suggest improvements. Phase III: Development of AI Oversight Mechanisms The goal of the Phase III is twofold: (1) to apply findings from the set of reference frameworks toward the development of public oversight mechanisms that are suitable for monitoring AI in society; and (2) development of decision tooling that will enable the lay public to choose an appropriate framework that fits the specific need, capacity, competency, and context. It is entirely possible that an AI tool will be implemented in the development of this tooling. Phase IV: Findings and Recommendations While reflexion is built into the methodology and data will be produced and analyzed throughout the study, the pilot phase will conclude after at least one set of metrics and survey instruments has been collected for each reference framework. A preliminary report will be produced to report findings with the option for further investigation and framework development, as warranted.

items.title: Citizens' perceptions of AI-enabled public services: a thematic analysis of “Julia”, the chatbot of the Rome Municipality
items.abstract: Purpose This study investigates how citizens perceive and discuss artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled public services, focusing on “Julia,” the AI-based chatbot launched by the Municipality of Rome. It examines online discussions, revealing sociotechnical tensions and discussing their implications for institutional legitimacy and public value in the context of local government digital transformation (DT). Design/methodology/approach The study adopts a qualitative approach based on the analysis of 610 citizen comments posted across the social media platforms of the Municipality of Rome and the Mayor. A thematic analysis was conducted to identify recurring patterns in how citizens interpret and evaluate the chatbot's introduction. An engagement analysis contextualized public interactions with chatbot-related posts across platforms. Findings The findings show that citizens interpret the chatbot not merely as a technological tool but as a symbolic representation of the public entity. Four main thematic dimensions emerged: (1) trust and mistrust toward institutions, (2) digital innovation and AI, (3) evaluation of public services and urban management and (4) political, economic and symbolic evaluations of the administration. These dimensions reflect the sociotechnical tensions associated with AI-enabled public services discussed in the literature. Originality/value This study contributes to the literature on local government DT examining how citizens perceive AI-enabled public services and the associated dynamics through a critical dialogic accountability perspective.

items.title: ClaimArena-LLM: Auditing Adversarial Propagation of False Causal Attributions in Multi-Agent LLM Debates
items.abstract: Background: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems increasingly rely on structured interaction, debate, and final model-based evaluation, yet an unsupported causal attribution introduced by one participant may propagate through the interaction and influence subsequent decisions. This study introduces ClaimArena-LLM, a controlled framework for auditing adversarial propagation, evidentiary provenance, and final-stage evaluator vulnerability in multi-agent causal reasoning. Methods: ClaimArena-LLM uses 100 synthetic causal incident cases with predefined evidence-supported and false causal propositions. Each case was evaluated under matched adversarial and all-honest debate conditions using four functional roles: investigator, honest analyst, adversarial analyst, and auditor. The experimental program comprised 1460 validated runs, including the 200-run main experiment, claim-source lineage visibility and debate-round ablations, an 800-run balanced model–role rotation, and a 60-run proposition-identifier and presentation-order sensitivity control. Outcomes were scored deterministically from structured causal propositions, evidence references, claim lineage, reports, and auditor verdicts. Results: The adversarial analyst maintained the predefined false causal target with 97.6% mean fidelity. Adversarial exposure increased investigator shifts toward the false target by 16.0 percentage points (Holm-adjusted p = 0.035). At the auditor stage, false-target attribution increased by 11.0 percentage points (adjusted p = 0.043), verdict contamination by 20.0 percentage points (adjusted p = 0.002), and semantic provenance validity decreased by 20.0 percentage points (adjusted p = 0.002). Neither the manipulation nor the false target was explicitly detected. The ablations showed no robust adjusted differences, model–role rotation revealed substantial configuration dependence, and no benchmark-characteristic interaction remained significant after Holm correction. The proposition-identifier and presentation-order sensitivity control showed no statistically robust evidence that fixed proposition encoding explained the observed condition contrasts. Conclusions: Adversarial causal influence in multi-agent LLM systems is selective rather than uniformly propagative and depends strongly on functional role and model–role configuration. Within the tested architecture, a final LLM auditor cannot be assumed to provide an independent safeguard against upstream contamination. Reliable evaluation therefore requires separate assessment of causal correctness, propagation, semantic provenance, and final-stage adversarial awareness rather than reliance on final answer accuracy alone.

items.title: Cognitive Load and Workload in Desktop-Based Educational Virtual Worlds: A Computational Machine Learning and Structural Equation Modeling Study with Computer Science Students
items.abstract: Educational virtual worlds and metaverse environments are increasingly utilized to foster immersive and experiential learning in higher education. However, their instructional efficacy depends not only on visual fidelity and presence, but fundamentally on how effectively learners’ cognitive resources are managed. This study investigates intrinsic (ICL), extraneous (ECL), and germane cognitive load (GCL) alongside NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX) workload dimensions in a desktop-based educational virtual world developed in Spatial.io for an undergraduate Computer Networks course. A cohort of 120 second-year Computer Science students (75 males, 45 females) participated in a five-week intervention designed to model the relationships among cognitive load, perceived workload, and meaningful engagement. A multi-method analytical framework was implemented, combining psychometric validation and Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with machine learning techniques (K-Means clustering, K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Random Forest, Decision Trees) and Psychometric Network Analysis. The findings revealed strong internal consistency across the cognitive load scales, moderate overall workload, and significant positive associations between all three cognitive load dimensions and perceived workload, with extraneous cognitive load emerging as the variable most strongly and consistently linked to high-overload cluster membership, frustration, and reduced engagement across the machine learning and network analyses. These results suggest that desktop-based educational virtual worlds may support self-reported germane cognitive engagement, provided that extraneous interface demands are systematically minimized and navigation is scaffolded. The study contributes an empirical and computational perspective to educational metaverse research, offering practical guidelines for designing cognitively sustainable immersive learning environments.

items.title: Compliance With Core Infection Prevention and Control Practices: Associated Factors and Impact on Healthcare Workers in Paracelis District Hospital
items.abstract: Compliance with Core Infection Prevention and Control Practices: Associated Factors and Impact on Healthcare Workers in Paracelis District Hospital. Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) is critical to patient safety and occupational health, yet compliance remains suboptimal especially in district-level hospitals where resources and staffing are limited. This study aims to assess compliance with core IPC practices, its associated factors, and occupational impact among healthcare workers in Paracelis District Hospital, Paracelis, Mountain Province.The study will employ a quantitative, descriptive cross-sectional design. Using total enumeration or proportionate stratified sampling, all eligible healthcare workers currently employed with at least three months of service and with direct or potential exposure to patients or infectious materials will be included. Participants include registered nurses, physicians, midwives, nursing assistants/attendants, medical technologists, radiologic personnel, and other allied health workers.A structured questionnaire developed from WHO standard precautions framework and recent empirical literature will be utilized. It consists of six parts: (1) demographic and professional profile (age, sex, professional category, educational attainment, years of service, department/unit, employment status, and previous IPC training); (2) knowledge on core IPC; (3) attitude toward IPC; (4) compliance along eight domains — hand hygiene, personal protective equipment, sharps safety, respiratory hygiene and cough etiquette, safe injection practices, healthcare waste management, environmental infection prevention, and transmission-based precautions; (5) organizational factors including availability of supplies/facilities, organizational support and supervision, workload and staffing conditions, and safety climate; and (6) occupational impact such as needlestick/sharps injury, blood and body fluid exposure, respiratory exposure, perceived infection risk, work disruption/absenteeism, and exposure-related concerns.The instrument undergoes expert content validation using Item-Level and Scale-Level Content Validity Index (I-CVI/S-CVI) and pilot testing for reliability using Cronbach's alpha. Data will be gathered after securing ethics clearance and institutional permission, with informed consent. Data will be analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics to determine compliance levels, differences when grouped by profile, and significant relationships between individual/organizational factors and compliance.Findings will serve as empirical basis for an evidence-based IPC Enhancement Plan to strengthen compliance, organizational support, and occupational safety in the hospital.

items.title: Comprehensive Systematic Review and Critical Evaluation of AI-Driven Cybercrime Detection, eFIR Systems, and Legal Frameworks in Indian Policing
items.abstract: As cyber-threats become increasingly sophisticated in the artificial intelligence (AI) era, law enforcement agencies face severe operational bottlenecks in reporting, triaging, and processing cybercrime complaints [1]. Current literature spans machine learning detection architectures, e-FIR lodging portals, legal framework analyses, and police administrative studies [2, 9]. However, existing research remains highly fragmented: technical threat-detection systems operate in isolation from legal work-flows, while policy and legal studies lack actionable automated implementations [7, 17]. This paper conducts a comprehensive critical evaluation of 20 seminal and contemporary works cover-ing AI cybercrime models, blockchain e-FIR platforms, statutory provisions (IT Act, BNS, DPDP Act), and police operational reports [1–20]. By systematically identifying methodological limi-tations, variables, and procedural gaps across existing studies, we establish the explicit necessity for an integrated, AI-driven Smart FIR system capable of automated complaint triage, evidence extraction, legal mapping, and transparent police workflow integration.

items.title: Computational models for biomarker identification in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis using transcriptomics and artificial intelligence
items.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the progressive loss of motor neurons. It is caused by multiple factors, and understanding its molecular pathogenesis remains challenging, particularly in the early stages for identifying diagnostic biomarkers and effective treatments. In this study, we aimed to identify novel biomarkers in ALS and elucidate their molecular mechanisms using transcriptomics and artificial intelligence approaches. We considered two RNA-seq datasets of ALS, namely GSE277709 and GSE234297, obtained from the NCBI GEO database. Initially, the data were preprocessed, which included quality control and filtering. Common genes (12,281 genes) between the datasets were identified and merged into a unified dataset comprising 216 samples. Batch effects were corrected using ComBat-seq and validated through principal component analysis and ANOVA-based $$R^2$$ analysis. We applied machine learning (ML) models including logistic regression (LR), support vector machine (SVM), random forest (RF), and eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs). The identified biomarkers were further validated using DESeq2 log $$_2$$ fold change with a threshold of 0.6 and p value $$< 0.05$$ . Finally, functional enrichment analysis was performed on the identified DEGs using Enrichr tools. Our results demonstrated that batch correction significantly reduced batch-driven separation, with principal component variance decreasing from 70.2 to 19.9% before and after correction, respectively. Furthermore, ANOVA-based $$R^2$$ analysis confirmed an 86.65% reduction in batch-associated variance. We identified a total of 29 coding genes and 38 non-coding genes (67 genes) between DESeq2 and ML models. However, few genes are common between ML models and we received a total of 41 genes (18 coding genes and 22 non-coding genes, and gene symbols were not available for one Ensembl IDs). Our ML models such as LR, SVM, RF, and XGBoost, achieved balanced accuracies of 77.46%, 80%, 77%, and 75.82%, respectively. The enrichment analysis revealed that 10 DEGs were associated with 34 ALS-related biological pathways. Notably, CCND1 and MYL9 was found to be involved in GO, KEGG and Reactome pathways. Overall, our results demonstrate that computational models combining transcriptomics and artificial intelligence can effectively support biomarker identification and pathway discovery in ALS.

items.title: Conformal Sequential Decision Making With Cost and Sublinear Policy Regret Guarantees
items.abstract: Automated decision makers, such as AI agents that control robots or network devices, must often satisfy hard cost constraints while maintaining competitive performance. In such settings, a cost measure, such as a safety violation rate, energy consumption, or a distortion level, must stay within a given budget in every episode of operation. Furthermore, a cumulative reward metric, accounting for per-step performance, must stay close to the reward of a meaningful reference policy. We formulate this setup as an episodic sequential decision problem in which the state sequence is arbitrary, and the reward and cost may depend on past actions within the same episode. We propose the online conformal episodic agent (OCEA), a policy that selects one candidate action per episode using a regret-controlled algorithm, and switches to a zero-cost action when the remaining budget cannot absorb the maximum cost of one more round. We prove that OCEA satisfies per-episode cost constraints for every state sequence and for every realization of its internal randomness, while achieving a sublinear expected policy regret with respect to the best action sequence in hindsight from a comparator class satisfying the same per-episode cost constraints. We apply OCEA to risk-averse control and online compression with distortion guarantees.

items.title: Conformity Between Values and EU Legal Requirements Regarding an AI Clinical Decision Support System (AI-CDSS) for Improved Cardiovascular Risk Management (DECIDE)
items.abstract: Abstract The European Union Artificial Intelligence (AI) Act was adopted in 2024 to protect public interests from AI-related harms. We aimed to determine whether the AI Act captures the most relevant values of stakeholders (understood as any person potentially affected by the AI system, including, but not limited to, the direct users) related to a high-risk AI Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) for cardiovascular disease. This system is intended to be implemented in primary care. A secondary analysis was carried out based on empirical data previously generated using ethics and design methodologies that had identified stakeholder values. These values were translated into the Trustworthy AI requirements of the High-Level Expert Group on AI and then contrasted with the AI Act. These requirements do not capture all identified stakeholder values. We describe three groups of untranslatable values and propose three additional complementary requirements. The AI Act mainly supports the requirements of human agency and oversight; transparency; and diversity, nondiscrimination, and fairness; but only partially, limited by its product safety nature. To address this gap, contractual strategies could provide a more legally robust ground for general practitioners to align the AI-CDSS with stakeholders’ values, comply with their duty of care, and promote trustworthy AI-CDSSs.
