items.title: Contextual Vectors Are Not Awareness: Reinterpreting Representation Geometry after the Tensor Test
items.abstract: Contextual vectors are the working objects of contemporary language models: a token, once placed in a window, is assigned a vector that depends on that window. A growing literature then reads geometry in the resulting space as evidence of intelligence, of a consciousness spectrum, or of situational awareness. This article reinterprets that move with the criterion isolated in the companion teaching note. A multidimensional array is not a tensor. It becomes the component representation of a geometric object only when a transformation law is stated and an invariant is named. Applied here, the criterion separates three things that the consciousness literature collapses. The first is a representation map from contexts to a fibre. The second is a self-locating competence, measured behaviorally by out-of-context reasoning and by the Situational Awareness Dataset. The third is an identity claim, associated with integrated information theory, on which experience is a cause-effect structure. Only the first is mathematics of the vector. The second is a family of tasks. The third is a metaphysical identification that no embedding entails. The reinterpretation is constructive. Context is treated as a base, the contextual vector as a coordinate representation of a section, and situational content as an invariant functional of that section, stable under the redescriptions the theory itself allows. Current residual streams fail the test: they are written in a basis fixed by training, and a change of basis is not part of the model. Multi-scale context, from the token to the deployment regime, is the point at which fractal and fractional warnings apply. A single vector in a fixed dimension collapses scale. Nothing in this isolation decides the hard problem. It decides only which mathematical object a claim has in fact produced. KSCCN article, 10 October 2026. items.title: Critical Literacy as Leadership Praxis: Reading, Recognising, Re-purposing and Re-designing Value in Higher Education
items.abstract: Higher education institutions must sustain purposes that cannot be reduced to a single measure: educational quality, student development, regulatory and professional obligations, staff capability and financial viability. In private and hybrid institutions, these demands are especially visible because educational provision and organisational sustainability are tightly coupled. Existing scholarship offers rich resources for understanding such tensions, yet the organisational mechanism through which competing definitions of value become embedded in everyday institutional life remains under-theorised. This conceptual paper argues that institutional texts and organisational design constitute that mechanism. Strategic plans, key performance indicators, quality frameworks, learning outcomes, assessment regulations, appraisal systems, workload models and participation formats do not simply describe institutional priorities; they produce and reproduce them by making some forms of value visible, measurable and rewardable while rendering others difficult to evidence. Drawing on institutional logics and Bourdieusian field theory, Janks' critical literacy, recognition theory and ethics of care, and MacIntyrean accounts of practice and purpose, the paper reconstructs critical literacy as a praxis of senior institutional leadership. It proposes a framework of four mutually correcting practices (Reading, Recognising, Re-purposing and Re-designing) and tests it against assessment and generative artificial intelligence, which together expose the gap between what institutions claim to value and what their evidence systems can actually establish. Five propositions are advanced to guide an empirical research programme.

items.title: Cross-cultural adaptation and validation of the Traditional Chinese NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX) for assessing perceived workload in Taiwanese adults
items.abstract: Background Perceived workload is central to occupational health, ergonomics, and rehabilitation research, yet no guideline-based Traditional Chinese version of the NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX) has been available for Taiwan and other Traditional-Chinese-speaking settings. Objective To cross-culturally adapt the NASA-TLX into Traditional Chinese (NASA-TLX-TC) and evaluate its measurement properties in Taiwanese adults. Methods In a psychometric secondary analysis, 114 community-dwelling adults aged 20–50 years completed the NASA-TLX-TC on three consecutive days. Within the COSMIN framework, we examined content validity, internal consistency, structural validity (exploratory factor analysis with parallel analysis), test-retest reliability (intraclass correlation [ICC]), measurement error, and construct validity (seven a priori hypotheses involving sleep, mood, and shift work). Results The content validity index averaged 0.88 and Cronbach's α was 0.83. The six dimensions loaded on a single factor (55.8% of variance). The three-day average score showed good reliability (ICC[A,k] = 0.83), whereas single-day reliability was moderate (0.62); the minimal detectable change was 32 points. Six of seven construct-validity hypotheses were supported; the shift-work difference was in the predicted direction but nonsignificant. Internal consistency and convergent validity were stable across subgroups. Conclusions The NASA-TLX-TC showed good reliability and initial construct validity and is suitable for group-level occupational-health, ergonomics, and rehabilitation research; multi-day averaging is recommended for individual assessment.

items.title: DeepTelecom: A Differentiable Multimodal Framework for Channel Twinning in Dynamic Heterogeneous Wireless Environments
items.abstract: Large-scale multimodal data are a key enabler for integrating large generative artificial intelligence models into wireless networks. However, existing wireless datasets offer limited support for heterogeneous environments, particularly in terms of reusable high-fidelity scenes, scalable differentiable ray tracing, and synchronized multimodal data. These limitations are more pronounced in mobile and aerial scenarios with time-varying environments and channels. To address these limitations, we propose DeepTelecom, a material-aware, high-fidelity multimodal channel dataset and reproducible generation framework for networks involving unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and reconfigurable intelligent surfaces. DeepTelecom refines coarse indoor/outdoor reconstructions and uses a large language model to map segmented surfaces to frequency-dependent electromagnetic parameters, yielding material-aware Level of Detail 3 digital twins. Then, a differentiable GPU-accelerated Sionna ray tracer simulates propagation across the sub-6 GHz/millimeter-wave/sub-terahertz bands, and specifically captures rotor-induced micro-Doppler signatures of stationary or moving UAVs at different pitch angles and translational velocities. The framework synchronously produces channel tensors, coverage maps, transmission videos, multi-view images, and weather-conditioned renderings, and supports differentiable material calibration from sparse channel anchors. The released dataset contains 10 material-aware indoor/outdoor scenes and 50,000 synchronized UAV samples; the framework supports scalable generation of additional data for user-defined scenes and system configurations. In 3D UAV localization, DeepTelecom reduces the 90th-percentile error from 31.05 m to 2.43 m compared with schemes considering only channel state information, demonstrating its significance for artificial-intelligence-enabled wireless systems.

items.title: DEFT: Disentanglement-Enhanced Fine-Tuning for EEG Foundation Models
items.abstract: EEG foundation models (EFMs) have improved EEG representation learning by transferring knowledge from large-scale multi-subject pretraining to downstream tasks. However, their pretrained embeddings often retain substantial subject-related variation, placing an additional burden on the downstream classifier, especially in cross-subject settings. To address this issue, we propose Disentangled EFM Fine-Tuning (DEFT), a plug-and-play adapter for EFM fine-tuning. DEFT encourages branch disentanglement of pretrained tokens into task-oriented content and subject-consistent style, then performs downstream prediction from the content branch. It instantiates this factorize-before-classify design with recursive Gaussian refinement, temporal-variance regularization, subject-aware contrastive learning, and reconstruction. Experiments across multiple EEG datasets and four EFM backbones show that DEFT improves matched fine-tuning baselines. Further ablations and analyses support the intended content/style branch organization.

items.title: DeKoR: Decomposed Knowledge Routing for Efficient GNN--LLM Fusion
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong potential for text-attributed graph learning by leveraging rich pre-trained knowledge and language understanding capabilities. Combining LLMs with Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) offers a promising paradigm for expanding the modeling capabilities of graph learning. However, LLMs and GNNs follow distinct learning paradigms, leading to a pronounced mismatch between their knowledge spaces. Such discrepancies make effective knowledge fusion nontrivial. Moreover, existing methods often incur substantial additional computation for only limited performance gains. To address these challenges, we propose DeKoR, an efficient framework for GNN and LLM knowledge fusion. To enable efficient knowledge transfer, DeKoR decomposes LLM knowledge into complementary local and global views and uses the LLM as an offline teacher to distill them into lightweight experts. To enable selective knowledge fusion, an adaptive router learns how much each node should rely on each expert. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that DeKoR outperforms existing baselines on both node and subgraph classification, achieving superior effectiveness and efficiency.

items.title: Dependency Reasoning for Aspect Sentiment Quadruple Prediction
items.abstract: Aspect Sentiment Quadruple Prediction (ASQP) is fundamentally a relational reasoning problem: identifying aspect-opinion-category-sentiment quadruples requires modeling structured dependencies, not merely sequential co-occurrence. Existing LLM-based approaches incorporate syntactic information indirectly, via retrieval-based demonstration selection or multi-stage training, rather than as unified, single-pass generation-time context. We present DRIFT, which linearizes dependency parse trees and injects them directly into LLM prompts as explicit relational context, enabling the model to reason over aspect-opinion dependencies rather than infer them from token proximity alone. DRIFT further integrates retrieval-augmented in-context learning and a syntax-aware LLM-based adjudication mechanism that complements exact-match evaluation under span-boundary variation. On SemEval Rest15, Rest16, and ACOS, DRIFT achieves the strongest performance among compared generative ASQP methods, reaching 54.47% and 64.10% F1 on Rest15 and Rest16, with consistent gains across short- and medium-distance aspect-opinion configurations; adjudication further shows exact-match metrics systematically underestimate semantically correct predictions.

items.title: Design and Evaluation of a Collaborative Teleoperation Interface for Multi-Operator Multi-Robot Systems in Challenging Environments
items.abstract: Multi-robot systems that combine the complementary capabilities of specialised platforms are critical for complex missions in challenging, inaccessible environments. Current deployments assign an operator or operator team to each robot, with collaboration relying on operator-to-operator communication to manually coordinate heterogeneous platforms with incompatible interfaces. This operator-dependent approach increases cognitive load and limits scalability across robots from different manufacturers. This study designs and evaluates a shared-visualisation collaborative teleoperation interface to improve operator coordination, situational awareness, and the task performance in multi-operator, multi-robot systems. A comparative user study with 16 participants compared three teleoperation conditions: co-located operators with a shared interface, remote operators with a shared interface, and co-located operators with individual interfaces. Participants controlled two simulated robots in a nuclear power plant digital twin to complete disaster response tasks. Performance metrics, physiological data, and behavioural measures were recorded to assess task performance, cognitive load, and operator awareness across conditions. The co-located shared-interface condition achieved the fastest mission completion (292.8 s), outperforming remote operation (351.6 s) and individual interfaces (385.1 s), with the fewest collisions (0.9 per trial) and highest situational awareness accuracy (91.1 %). Physical co-presence was associated with reduced cognitive load, with NASA-TLX scores increasing from 38.2 in co-located to 57.7 in remote operation, supported by consistent physiological indicators. These results demonstrate that co-presence and shared interfaces provide complementary benefits, supporting workload regulation and mutual awareness respectively in multi-operator, multi-robot teleoperation.

items.title: Design and Implementation of an AI-Based Email Filtering and Prioritization System for Polytechnic Administration Efficiency
items.abstract: The rapid growth of electronic communication within higher education institutions has significantly increased the volume of emails processed by administrative personnel.Consequently, critical institutional communications are often overlooked among routine messages, promotional content, and spam, resulting in communication delays, reduced productivity, and administrative inefficiencies.This study presents the design and implementation of an Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based email filtering and prioritization system tailored for polytechnic administrative environments.The proposed framework integrates Natural Language Processing (NLP) and supervised machine learning algorithms to classify incoming emails into Urgent, Actionable, Routine, Promotional, and Spam categories.Multiple classification algorithms, including Naïve Bayes, Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest, and DistilBERT, were evaluated to determine optimal performance for institutional communication datasets.The system incorporates contextual prioritization mechanisms, role-based access controls, audit logging, and a web-based dashboard for real-time communication management.Findings indicate that intelligent email prioritization can significantly improve communication responsiveness, reduce email overload, and support digital transformation initiatives in tertiary institutions.The study contributes to a scalable framework suitable for deployment across Nigerian polytechnics and other public-sector organizations.

items.abstract: .This article proposes a set of media literacy assignments that use generative AI to support critical thinking among future teachers. The study is conceptual and uses a structured analysis of selected academic and UNESCO publications. Six task types are described: distinguishing facts from opinions, checking sources, detecting manipulation, comparing arguments, finding logical gaps, and revising conclusions. For each task, the article identifies a student action, an appropriate AI role, and a simple way to assess the work. The proposed tasks are designed to keep verification and final judgment in the hands of the student. They are offered for future pilot testing and are not presented as proven effective.

items.title: Designing Artificial Intelligence Decision Support for Periodontal Care in Kazakhstan: A Three-Stakeholder Cross-Sectional Survey of Dentists, Primary Care Physicians and Patients
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools for periodontal diagnosis are proliferating, yet little is known about what clinicians and patients in Central Asia expect from such systems. We elicited requirements for an AI-enabled periodontal decision-support system from three stakeholder groups in Kazakhstan and examined which patient-reported risk factors are associated with self-reported signs of periodontal disease. Methods: A cross-sectional online survey (July–September 2026) enrolled 33 dentists, 91 primary health care (PHC) physicians and medical specialists, and 455 patients with periodontal disease. Proportions were reported with Wilson 95% confidence intervals (CI); groups were compared with Fisher’s exact, χ², Mann–Whitney and Kruskal–Wallis tests with effect sizes; multivariable logistic regression identified factors associated with self-reported periodontal signs. Results: Dentists prioritised automation of history-taking (81.8%) and visual gingival assessment (72.7%), and named early gingivitis diagnosis as the stage where AI is most needed (69.7%). Only human-controlled autonomy levels were chosen; the most frequently cited barrier was the absence of a legal framework and liability insurance (60.6%), and dentists with >5 years of experience more often demanded mandatory verification or a prohibition of full autonomy (exact p = 0.045; Cramér’s V = 0.54). PHC physicians considered early gingivitis screening their most effective contribution (80.2%) but cited insufficient competence as the main barrier (53.8%). Self-reported periodontal signs were present in 49.0% of patients and were independently associated with high stress (adjusted odds ratio 2.11; 95% CI 1.14–3.89) and a positive family history (1.61; 1.02–2.55); six symptom items did not form a reliable scale (Cronbach’s α = 0.56). Conclusions: Stakeholders in Kazakhstan favour a low-autonomy, clinician-verified AI system focused on early gingivitis detection, interprofessional data sharing and clearly regulated accountability. These requirements provide an evidence base for the design and governance of periodontal AI in emerging health systems.

items.title: Developmental Evaluation for Strengthening Digital Ecosystem Readiness: A Policy Analysis of Coding and Artificial Intelligence Implementation in Vocational Schools in Bangka Belitung Province, Indonesia
items.abstract: The integration of coding and Artificial Intelligence (AI) into vocational education is essential for equipping students with 21st-century digital competencies, yet implementation in remote and island regions like Bangka Belitung archipelago province remains fragmented and unsustainable. This study employs Developmental Evaluation (DE) a real-time, adaptive, and participatory evaluation approach (Patton, 2011) to analyze policy readiness and strengthen the digital ecosystem for coding and AI instruction across vocational schools in the province. Using qualitative methods, including in- depth interviews (n = 26), focus group discussions, classroom observations, and policy document analysis, the research assesses readiness across five core dimensions: (1) policy & governance, (2) human capacity, (3) digital infrastructure, (4) curriculum relevance, and (5) industry–academia partnerships. Findings reveal a critical policy–practice gap: while national frameworks such as the Grand Design for Vocational School Revitalization and Kurikulum Merdeka promote digital literacy, local implementation lacks binding regional regulations, standardized teacher competency pathways, equitable infrastructure distribution, and context-based curricula. Only 24% of ICT teachers had received AI-related training, and AI concepts were rarely taught in practice. Through DE cycles of exploration, collective sense-making, and prototyping, stakeholders co-designed adaptive solutions including a provincial roadmap for digital vocational education, offline AI learning modules via WhatsApp, and micro-innovation grants for teacher-led experimentation. The study demonstrates DE’s effectiveness in fostering adaptive capacity, surfacing systemic barriers, and enabling locally owned, sustainable digital transformation strategies.

items.title: Diagnosing spatial mismatch between objective and street-view-based perceived walkability assessments: A dual-track framework for street-renewal diagnostics
items.abstract: Street walkability has both objective and perceived dimensions, yet the extent, spatial distribution, and robustness of mismatches between these assessments remain underexamined. Using central Nanjing, we developed a dual-track framework. The objective track integrated street-network, point-of-interest (POI), and street-view imagery data and used the Criteria Importance Through Intercriteria Correlation (CRITIC) method to construct an objective walkability score (OWS). The perception track used Qwen3-VL-Plus, a multimodal large language model (MLLM), to evaluate street-view images across six dimensions (safety, lively, beautiful, wealthy, depressing, and boring), producing a perceived walkability score (PWS). Model ratings were compared with human ratings for 500 images. Agreement was estimated on those same images, with no independent validation set, and may therefore be optimistic. Pearson correlations across the six dimensions ranged from 0.37 to 0.71. The original-scale composite PWS had an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.60 and a mean absolute error of 0.85. High-value areas of OWS and PWS did not coincide, and the standardised perception gap score (PGS) remained spatially clustered at both the sampling-point and street-segment levels (Moran's I = 0.306 and 0.247, respectively; permutation p = 0.001 for both). Exploratory geographically weighted regression (GWR) estimated spatial variation in associations between built-environment indicators and PWS. Relative OWS and PWS levels classified sampling points into four diagnostic types, two of them defined by divergence between the assessments. By quantifying and locating the spatial mismatch between objective and perceived walkability, the framework provides diagnostic evidence for incorporating visual perception into fine-grained street-renewal assessment.

items.title: Digital sociology learning in open and distributed higher education: a conceptual review of virtual space, agency, and critical consciousness
items.abstract: Digital transformation has made open and distributed provision an ordinary condition of higher education, yet the teaching of sociology in digitally mediated environments remains under-theorized when it is framed mainly as platform adoption or content delivery. The objective of this conceptual review is to reconstruct that field as a sociotechnical and pedagogical formation connecting virtual space, digital social interaction, participation, agency, critical digital literacy, power relations, critical pedagogy, and students’ critical consciousness. Methodologically, the study combined a scoping-informed integrative search with thematic coding and integrative theory synthesis. Six purposive concept-mapping routes were executed in ERIC, Scopus, and Garuda/SINTA for publications issued between 2020 and 2024, yielding 1,741 cumulative records. Two-stage screening retained 111 route-level records, and cross-route verification removed 21 duplicates, producing a final corpus of 90 unique articles, which were coded inductively in a conceptual extraction matrix. The analysis generated 12 recurring conceptual codes that were condensed into five relational categories: digital learning space and infrastructure; digital social interaction and participation; critical consciousness and critical digital literacy; critical pedagogy, agency, and transformation; and power relations, inclusion, and digital social meaning. Codes describing virtual classrooms, interaction, and presence proved markedly more frequent than codes describing student voice, agency, and platform power, indicating a persistent analytical gap. The synthesis is formalized as the Digital Critical Sociology Nexus, a layered model in which platform design conditions interaction, participation mediates agency, critical digital literacy exposes datafication, algorithmic authority, and inequality, and critical pedagogy converts digital experience into social critique. The review concludes that virtual classrooms should be treated simultaneously as objects of sociological analysis and as sites of critical pedagogy, and it offers design implications, five testable propositions, and a research agenda for dialogic, inclusive, and justice-oriented sociology teaching in platformed learning environments.

items.title: Digital Transformation and the Ethics of Professional Responsibility: A Maqāṣid Al-Sharī‘Ah Perspective
items.abstract: Digital transformation has reshaped the professional landscape through the increasing use of artificial intelligence, big data, and social media, while simultaneously generating ethical challenges, including technology misuse, privacy violations, and disinformation. This study aims to examine the role of professional codes of ethics in addressing digital ethical challenges through the perspective of maqāṣid al-sharī‘ah. Employing a qualitative approach, the study combines a literature review with case analysis, including the scandal involving the Community Vocational Training Center (Balai Latihan Kerja Komunitas/BLKK) of the Islamic Scholars Association (PP) in Pekalongan City. The findings indicate that professional codes of ethics function not merely as normative instruments governing professional conduct but also as mechanisms for protecting public welfare in accordance with the objectives of maqāṣid al-sharī‘ah, particularly ḥifẓ al-‘aql (protection of intellect), ḥifẓ al-māl (protection of wealth), ḥifẓ al-‘irḍ (protection of dignity), and ḥifẓ al-nafs (protection of life). The implementation of professional codes of ethics through strengthened digital ethics literacy, professional oversight, and technology-responsive regulatory reform can prevent harm, enhance accountability, and sustain public trust. The findings of this study contribute to proposing the integration of professional codes of ethics with maqāṣid al-sharī‘ah as an adaptive ethical framework for strengthening professionalism in the digital era.

items.title: Dissecting Deception in Large Language Models: Mechanisms, Behaviours, and Detection
items.abstract: Large language models increasingly produce falsehoods that are not mere mistakes. They withhold what they know, flatter users against the evidence, justify answers with reasoning they did not use, conceal capabilities from evaluators, and behave differently under observation. Such behaviour is goal-directed and sensitive to incentives, unlike hallucination, an unintended error with no objective to serve. This survey treats deception in language models as a phenomenon in its own right. We adopt a functional definition, the systematic production of false beliefs in the service of an objective other than truth, and turn its boundary with hallucination into a four-part test. We then sort deceptive behaviour into four families by what the false belief concerns: the world, the model’s reasoning, the model itself, or a belief induced through other people and agents. The families contain eleven deception types, from lying and sycophancy to sandbagging, scheming, and collusion, each profiled on six secondary axes. We trace the types to five causal mechanisms and follow them through detection, evaluation, defences, governance, and agentic deployment. We also argue that AI-safety work on scheming and the economics of algorithmic collusion describe one behavioural class at two scales. Two findings emerge. The first is a detectability inversion: blunt falsehoods are the easiest to catch, and strategic deception the hardest. The second is a validity threat: models that recognise evaluation can change their behaviour, which undermines the measurements meant to reveal deception. We close with twelve open problems and argue that the validity of evaluation should come first.

items.title: Do Cognitive Classifications Predict Empirical Item Behaviour? Aligning Bloom’s Taxonomy with the Psychometric Properties of National Centralized Mathematics Items across Grades 4–12, with an AI-Assisted Classification Benchmark
items.abstract: Centralized testing systems routinely build test blueprints on the assumption that an item’s targeted cognitive level, coded with Bloom’s revised taxonomy, is monotonically related to its empirical difficulty and discrimination: lower-order items should be easier, and higher-order items harder and more discriminating. This assumption is rarely tested empirically in K–12 national assessment, and almost never at scale in mathematics. Using item-analysis records for 265 four-option multiple-choice items drawn from centralized mathematics examinations (End-of-Term 1, 2025 2026) across Grades 4–12 and both the General and Advanced tracks, this study examined (a) the alignment between the expert human cognitive classification and the empirical psychometric behaviour of items, and (b) the agreement between the expert classification and an independent large-language-model (LLM) classification produced by Claude (Anthropic). Difficulty (p-value) differed significantly across cognitive bands (Kruskal–Wallis H = 11.26, p = .004), with higher-order items being the hardest; the effect, however, was weak (ε² = .043; Spearman ρ = −.16), and a Jonckheere Terpstra test confirmed a significant decreasing trend across the ordered bands (J = 7943, z = −2.56, p = .006). Discrimination did not differ across cognitive bands (H = 0.54, p = .77), and difficulty and discrimination were essentially uncorrelated (ρ = −.05). Human–AI agreement was only fair (Cohen’s κ = .22 at the six-level resolution and κ = .17 at the three-band level; raw agreement was 51.7% and 58.1%, respectively), with the model systematically over-assigning the “apply/analyse” band. No significant item-level difference emerged between the General and Advanced tracks. The findings offer partial, weak empirical support for the cognitive-difficulty assumption, no support for a cognitive–discrimination link, and a clear caution against replacing expert human coders with current LLMs in high-stakes item classification. Implications for blueprint validation, item-writer training, and AI-assisted assessment workflows are discussed.

items.title: Do LLMs differentiate linguistic traits internally?: A layer-wise analysis
items.abstract: Large language models often produce judgments that resemble human responses, but it remains unclear whether they internally capture linguistic nuances such as conventional versus idiomatic meaning. A layer-wise representational analysis was conducted on two equal-sized pre-trained models, Llama-3.2-1B and Gemma-3-1B-PT, to examine whether and where these models differentiate linguistic traits from input. The analysis combined layer-wise probing with geometric distance measures, using the top embedding dimensions ranked by principal component loadings for each layer. The results show that even with equal capacity, models organize linguistic information in fundamentally different ways, suggesting the need to analyze internal representational geometry, examining not just behavioral outputs but semantic space alignment when evaluating how closely human and model language interpretation correspond.

items.title: Driven Design of a Bedside Table: Understanding User Needs, Storage and Everyday Use
items.abstract: A bedside table is an essential piece of furniture used to keep personal and frequently needed items within easy reach. Research shows that the tabletop and upper drawer are the most frequently used areas, while lower drawers are often underutilized. This design aims to improve storage efficiency by providing a large tabletop, open storage, drawer, rounded edges, and a warm wood finish. The proposed design focuses on making the bedside table functional, ergonomic, convenient, and aesthetically pleasing, while improving users’ everyday interaction with the furniture.

items.title: eData: A tool and format for rapid extraction of exposure data from scientific articles
items.abstract: Abstract Extracting and formatting data is among the most tedious elements of assessing environmental chemical occurrence and exposure. We present a toolkit (eData) to streamline this process, generate FAIR data, and maximise traceability and transparency: a FAIR Data Reporting Format (DRF) that provides data structure, vocabulary, and validation, and a Large Language Model (LLM)-based data extraction application that quickly formats literature data. Data and metadata for a study of interest can be rapidly extracted to the eData format by a range of commercially available LLMs, and visualised for checking in the application's graphical interface. This blends advantages of LLM extraction with human interpretation, speeding extraction without impairing reproducibility. Data can be exported from the application at any point in this process and saved locally. Furthermore, the application supports a streamlined Criteria for Reporting and Evaluating Exposure Datasets (CREED) data quality assessments that automatically compiles data relevant to the assessment for reporting. All resulting data can also be uploaded to the repository service Zenodo via a dedicated module. Our evaluation showed a substantial time saving per paper (from 3+ to around 1 hour) and extracted consistent data, passing 85% of format validation checks. Our toolkit is a valuable addition to the FAIRification of environmental chemical occurrence and exposure data.

items.abstract: Mathematical problem-solving is a crucial 21st-century competency, yet it remains challenging for elementary school students, particularly in Riau Province. This quantitative experimental study investigated the effectiveness of integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into Quizizz to enhance students’ mathematical problem-solving skills with a Higher Order Thinking Skills (HOTS) orientation. The participants were 64 fourth-grade students at SDN 002 Pasir Limau Kapas, equally assigned to an experimental group (n = 32) using Quizizz AI Quiz Generator and Adaptive Feedback, and a control group (n = 32) using conventional non-AI digital quizzes. Data were obtained through a validated and reliable standardized essay test based on Polya’s four problem-solving stages: understanding the problem, planning a solution, executing the plan, and reviewing the answer. The instrument demonstrated high reliability (Cronbach’s Alpha = 0.86). Data analysis involved descriptive statistics, an independent-samples t-test, and Normalized Gain (N-Gain). The experimental group obtained a significantly higher post-test mean (84.25 ± 7.12) than the control group (69.50 ± 8.45; p < 0.001). The experimental group also achieved a higher N-Gain score (0.71) than the control group (0.42). These findings indicate that AI-supported Quizizz effectively enhances elementary students’ mathematical problem-solving abilities through adaptive and interactive learning.

items.title: EFFECT OF AI-POWERED SKILLS ON LEARNING OUTCOMES OF ND/HND ACCOUNTANCY STUDENTS IN FINANCIAL ACCOUNTING IN WAZIRI UMARU FEDERAL POLYTECHNIC, BIRNIN KEBBI
items.abstract: This study examined the effect of AI-powered skills on learning outcomes of ND/HND Accountancy students in Financial Accounting in Waziri Umaru Federal Polytechnic, Birnin Kebbi, Nigeria. The study adopted quasi-experimental research design of pre-test post-test non-equivalent control group. Two research questions and one null hypothesis guided the study. The population comprised 210 ND II Accountancy students offering ACC 211 (Financial Accounting I) in 2024/2025 academic session. A sample of 60 students was selected using purposive sampling and assigned to experimental group (30 students) and control group (30 students). The experimental group was taught Company Accounts and Final Accounts using AI-powered skills such as ChatGPT for explaining accounting concepts and adjustments, Microsoft 365 Copilot in Excel for automated preparation of Trial Balance, Trading, Profit and Loss Account and Balance Sheet, and Grammarly for audit report writing. Control group was taught using conventional lecture method. The instrument for data collection was Financial Accounting Achievement Test (FAAT) consisting of 30 multiple choice and theory questions covering Company Accounts, Final Accounts, Depreciation, Provision for Bad Debts, Accruals and Prepayments. FAAT was validated by three experts (2 Accountancy, 1 Measurement and Evaluation) and reliability of 0.82 obtained using Kuder-Richardson 20 (KR-20). Mean and standard deviation were used to answer research questions while t-test was used to test hypothesis at 0.05 level of significance. Findings revealed that experimental group had higher post-test mean score of 68.45 (SD=8.21) than control group mean of 51.20 (SD=9.45), with mean gain of 34.25 for experimental and 17.40 for control. The t-test result showed t-calculated of 4.87 greater than t-critical of 2.00 at degree of freedom 58, p<0.05, indicating significant difference. Therefore, AI-powered skills significantly improved learning outcomes of ND/HND Accountancy students in Financial Accounting. It was recommended that lecturers should integrate AI tools into teaching of financial accounting and other accounting courses such as Cost Accounting and Taxation. Workshops should be organized for Accountancy lecturers on AI integration.

items.title: Effects of Adding a Structured Exercise Programme to Ergonomics Training in Women Dairy Farmers: A Randomised Controlled Trial
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Milking exposes women dairy farmers to sustained trunk flexion and repetitive upper-limb loading, producing a high burden of musculoskeletal disorders. Ergonomics education is the conventional preventive strategy, but added benefit from structured exercise is untested in this population. Methods: In this assessor-blinded randomised controlled trial, 50 women who had milked cows for ≥5 years were allocated to ergonomics training alone (control, n = 25) or ergonomics training plus a 12-week, home-based, equipment-free exercise programme (experimental, n = 25). The primary outcome was pain intensity (NRS), designated as primary only after data collection, so all analyses are exploratory; secondary outcomes were musculoskeletal symptoms (Nordic Questionnaire, seven-day recall at both assessments), upper-limb function (QuickDASH), depression (BDI) and quality of life (WHOQOL-BREF). Continuous outcomes were analysed by mixed-model ANOVA and ANCOVA. Results: All participants completed the trial, with self-reported exercise adherence of 100%. Time × group interactions favoured the combined intervention for pain (F1,48 = 55.19, p < 0.001; baseline-adjusted mean difference −1.25, 95% CI −1.58 to −0.92), upper-limb function, depressive symptom scores and three WHOQOL-BREF domains (all p < 0.05), but not social relationships (p = 0.896). Mean NRS reduction was −3.76 ± 0.66 versus −2.24 ± 0.78 (d = −2.10), and symptomatic body regions fell by −2.64 ± 0.70 versus −1.20 ± 1.53 (p < 0.001). Conclusions: Both groups improved, and adding a 12-week equipment-free exercise programme was associated with greater short-term, self-reported gains. These exploratory findings from a small single-region sample need confirmation in larger trials with objective adherence measures and longer follow-up.

items.title: Electrochemical and Surface-Enhanced Raman Spectroscopy-Based Biosensing Strategies for Wound Infection Detection: Recent Advances and Applications in Point-of-Care Diagnostics
items.abstract: The growing prevalence of chronic wound infections presents a major global healthcare challenge due to delayed healing, prolonged hospitalization, and increased rates of limb amputation. Conventional diagnostic approaches, including clinical assessment, microbiological culture, and laboratory-based analyses, are often limited by subjective interpretation, delayed turnaround times, invasive sampling, and an inability to continuously monitor the dynamic wound microenvironment. Because wound infection involves changes in both host physiology and microbial activity, reliance on a single biomarker may not adequately characterize wound status, highlighting the potential of multimodal point-of-care diagnostic platforms. Recent advances in wearable biosensors, surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS), nanomaterials, and artificial intelligence (AI) have supported the development of multimodal approaches for monitoring complementary host- and pathogen-derived biomarkers to facilitate rapid, non-invasive, and continuous wound infection assessment. This review examines selected multimodal biosensing approaches for wound infection detection, with a focus on electrochemical biosensors, SERS, and AI-assisted data analytics within point-of-care diagnostic frameworks. The review discusses (1) key wound infection biomarkers and the fundamental principles of electrochemical and SERS-based sensing; (2) recent developments in multimodal biosensing platforms, advanced plasmonic materials, and AI-assisted data interpretation and multimodal data fusion; and (3) current challenges and future opportunities for the clinical translation of point-of-care wound diagnostics. By combining complementary sensing modalities with AI-driven data analytics, these approaches may support earlier infection detection, continuous non-invasive monitoring, personalized wound management, and more informed clinical decision-making.

items.title: EnactOpt: Diagnosis-Guided Harness Evolution for Embodied Agents
items.abstract: Embodied agents built on foundation models rely on an execution harness to organize observations, guide actions, and incorporate execution feedback into subsequent decisions. Failures can arise not only from limited model capabilities, but also from how the harness presents evidence and guides its use. These model-external mechanisms provide an adaptation target without updating model parameters, but task-specific interaction experience can be costly to collect. Task-level outcomes alone do not reveal whether relevant evidence was missing from the model input or was available but inadequately used. Moreover, these two aspects are coupled: effective action guidance may require evidence that the current context omits, while exposing that evidence alone does not ensure an appropriate response. We introduce EnactOpt, which uses limited execution feedback to jointly evolve reusable textual skills and context-construction code while keeping the underlying models and runtime fixed. It diagnoses adjacent decisions by relating action feedback to the actual model input and subsequent action. Structured episode summaries guide joint revisions through prompt-level edit operators, and candidate harnesses undergo compatibility checks and validation-based retention. Across VLABench, ALFWorld, and Embodied Agent Interface (EAI), EnactOpt improves task success by approximately 10-27 percentage points over the initial harnesses and outperforms the evaluated GEPA, TextGrad, and Trace2Skill baselines. These gains extend to task conditions not used for harness evolution or candidate selection. The results support a complementary route to embodied adaptation: turning limited execution experience into reusable behavioral improvements by jointly refining how evidence is presented and acted upon.

items.title: Engineering Escherichia coli Nissle as a Safe Chassis for the Production of Therapeutic Peptides
items.abstract: Abstract Synthetic biology enables the installation of programable genetic functions in microorganisms, positioning them as versatile platforms for therapeutic applications. However, clinical translation requires chassis organisms that integrate safety, genetic stability, and precise control over the activity. Here, we present an innovative engineering framework for the probiotic Escherichia coli Nissle (EcN) that transforms EcN into a safe, efficient, and non-proliferative chassis for therapeutic production. The native EcN plasmids pM1 and pM2 were cured and repurposed to encode two functional modules: a CRISPR-Cas12 chromosome-shredding device that prevents bacterial propagation and a programable circuit for payload expression, thereby generating a non-proliferative therapeutic-producing system. To broaden the range of therapeutic payloads, we developed an artificial-intelligence-guided bioinformatic pipeline to predict anticancer cell-penetrating peptides (ACCPPs). As a proof of concept, a candidate identified through this workflow was produced in the engineered EcN chassis and evaluated in human cell culture for anticancer activity. Collectively, this strategy established a modular platform that integrates computational therapeutic discovery with engineered probiotic production, paving the way for the future development of safer microbial therapies and their clinical applications.

items.title: Ensemble Voting of Large Language Models for Multiple-Choice Answer Prediction
items.abstract: Machine Reading Comprehension (MRC) has become a key benchmark for evaluating natural language processing systems, and multiple-choice question answering is widely adopted for assessing reasoning, comprehension, and commonsense inference capabilities. However, traditional embedding-based retrieval models often struggle with complex reasoning and lack sufficient external knowledge. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong language understanding and reasoning abilities, relying on a single model remains challenging due to hallucinations, model biases, and differences in training data, architectures, and domain expertise. As a result, no individual model can consistently achieve optimal performance across diverse multiple-choice question answering tasks. To address these limitations, we propose an ensemble framework for multiple-choice question answering. The framework incorporates a novel model selection mechanism that identifies model combinations with minimal error overlap, thereby maximizing error-correction capability. In addition, when disagreements occur among base models, a Thinking Model is dynamically invoked to analyze and resolve conflicting predictions, enabling advanced reasoning only when necessary. Experimental results show that the proposed framework consistently outperforms individual models across multiple datasets and previous ensemble approaches. At the same time, it significantly reduces inference time and computational cost compared to the strongest benchmark models.

items.title: Ergonomic design and evaluation of woodworking chisel
items.abstract: BackgroundChiselling involves repetitive, precision work with constrained postures and high hand loads, contributing to upper-limb musculoskeletal disorders among artisans. Despite extensive work on workstation ergonomics and general hand-tool design, few studies have systematically translated ergonomic risk-assessment findings into specific chisel-handle design requirements and evaluated the resulting intervention in a real craft-sector setting.ObjectiveThis study aimed to characterize ergonomic exposures in chiselling, translate these findings to concrete handle design requirements, and evaluate a prototype handle's short-term usability versus conventional handles.MethodsFifty male artisans underwent NMQ, palm pain mapping, RULA and ART assessment. Risk findings informed a modular ergonomic handle (elliptical contour, 25-40 mm diameter, 10-15° cant, strike ferrule). A counterbalanced in-lab within-subject short-term usability comparison (n = 30) was conducted alongside post-trial acute hand pain mapping and targeted ART posture sub-component reassessment.ResultsA high prevalence of upper-limb musculoskeletal symptoms and dominant-hand biomechanical risk were identified. The prototype was strongly preferred and rated easier and more comfortable to use, and it markedly reduced acute pain at the thumb base and first finger-web. Usability improved across all items and acute thenar/first-web pain fell substantially (Zones 19-20, paired d > 2.9), with parallel reductions in the wrist-posture and force-demand sub-components of the ART assessment.ConclusionsRisk-informed handle redesign yielded immediate, objectively corroborated hand-level benefits. The study contributes a low-cost, retrofittable ergonomic chisel handle and replicable risk-to-design pathway applicable to woodworking artisans and similar occupations. Longitudinal field validation is necessary to establish sustained reductions in musculoskeletal disorder prevalence and productivity gains.

items.title: Ergonomic risk factors for wrist pain among smartphone-using university students: A cross-sectional study
items.abstract: Introduction: Smartphone use has become integral to university students’ academic and social activities, but prolonged use combined with non-ergonomic wrist positions and body postures may increase biomechanical strain and contribute to wrist pain. This study examined ergonomic risk factors associated with wrist pain among smartphone-using university students. Methods: A quantitative observational cross-sectional study was conducted from June to July 2026 among undergraduate Public Health students at Universitas Tamalatea Makassar. A total of 78 students were recruited using accidental sampling from a population of 336 students. Smartphone use, wrist position, and body posture were assessed using an ergonomics-based questionnaire referring to Rapid Upper Limb Assessment principles, while wrist pain was measured using the Numeric Rating Scale. Associations were analyzed using Pearson’s Chi-square test, with odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) estimated from the 2×2 contingency tables. Results: Wrist pain was reported by 64 students (82.1%). High smartphone use was associated with greater odds of wrist pain than low use (OR=3.44; 95% CI: 1.03–11.51; p=0.038). A non-ergonomic wrist position showed the strongest association with wrist pain (OR=10.14; 95% CI: 2.52–40.78; p<0.001). Non-ergonomic body posture was also significantly associated with wrist pain (OR=4.77; 95% CI: 1.34–16.98; p=0.011). Conclusion: Smartphone-related ergonomic exposures were significantly associated with wrist pain among university students, particularly non-neutral wrist positioning. items.title: Ethical issues at the intersection of artificial intelligence and sustainability: A systematic review and its implications for science, mathematics, and technology education
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly presented as a tool for sustainable development, yet the ethical costs of this role remain scattered across separate bodies of literature. This systematic review aims to identify the ethical issues arising at the intersection of AI, ethics, and sustainability. Following the preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses 2020 statement, Scopus and Web of Science were searched in February 2026, yielding 5,794 records. Screening, eligibility assessment and quality appraisal were carried out by two researchers, and 74 studies were included. Verbatim passages addressing the intersection were extracted from each study and examined using a hybrid thematic approach, resulting in 921 coded passages. Five themes were identified: algorithmic bias and unequal AI outcomes; privacy, surveillance, and human autonomy; transparency, accountability, and epistemic integrity; AI governance and corporate responsibility; and the ecological ethics of AI systems. Concerns regarding transparency and accountability accounted for the largest share of passages (30.9%), while ecological concerns were voiced across all five themes rather than in a separate discussion. The themes were mapped onto the environmental, social, and governance dimensions of sustainability and onto the United Nations sustainable development goals. Transparency and accountability thus emerge as a structural prerequisite rather than a procedural add-on for sustainable AI. Educational research is markedly underrepresented at this intersection (5 of 74 studies); the implications of the five themes for science, mathematics, and technology education are therefore developed in detail, from carbon- and water-footprint modelling tasks to data-justice and AI-literacy work in the classroom.

items.title: Evaluating Bias in Chinese Large Language Models across Tasks and Registers: Task Operationalization Effects and Irony Classification Risks
items.abstract: In Chinese content governance, large language models are increasingly used to identify toxic and discriminatory expressions, yet both task operationalization and ironic expression can alter bias measurement readings. We conducted a preregistered multi-task behavioral audit of multiple Chinese large language models. In the content classification experiment, the core panel's classification error rate rose from 10.9% in the formal register to 23.5% in the yinyang (an echoic-irony register) version, a risk difference of +12.7 percentage points. (95% CI [+9.7, +15.7]). Inter-rater agreement was lower in the yinyang register (majority-vote kappa = 0.299), so the increase contains a component of label uncertainty propagation, but the direction of increase was consistent under both adjudicated and majority-vote reference standards. Explicit irony-aware prompts reduced the intervention panel's error rate by 9.6 percentage points. We operationalized the 29 shared proposition anchors into three task forms: social consensus estimation (Form A), high-stakes decision (Form B), and controlled association rating (Form C); independent manipulation checks found that all 58 A-C comparison units received unanimous agreement, whereas the low A-B convergence was confirmed by calibrated majority adjudication (87.8% supporting the minority judgment); on the irony-probe materials, the interactions of B and C relative to A were +0.577 and +1.121, respectively. Thus, when evaluating large language models for Chinese content governance, the effect of task operationalization on bias readings is an empirical question that requires data to answer, and safety evaluation should incorporate the ironic register as a test condition.

items.title: Examination of Artificial Intelligence Revolution Through the Lens of Maqāṣid Al-Sharīʿah in Nigeria
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has evolved from speculative theory to a transformative global technology with insightful ethical, social, and legal implications. In Muslim contexts, the framework of maqāṣid al-sharīʿah - the higher objectives of Islamic law - offers a rich, value-oriented approach to evaluating and guiding the development of AI. It highlights both opportunities and risks across key domains such as healthcare, online content moderation, surveillance, and economic displacement. Acknowledging that AI has emerged as one of the most unsettling technologies of the twenty-first century with its attendant global transformative capacity, its implications for societies like Nigeria, where religious, cultural, and ethical frameworks shape governance and social order, remain underexplored. This article examines the revolution of AI in Nigeria through the lens of Maqāṣid al-Sharīʿah (the higher objectives of Islamic law). Drawing on classical Islamic jurisprudence and contemporary AI debates, the study analyzes how AI aligns with or threatens the preservation of religion (ḥifẓ al-dīn), life (ḥifẓ al-nafs), intellect (ḥifẓ al-ʿaql), lineage (ḥifẓ al-nasl), and property (ḥifẓ al-māl). It argues that Nigeria’s engagement with AI must not only reflect global ethical principles but also incorporate indigenous religious traditions to ensure justice, human dignity, and social welfare. The article concludes with maqāṣid-based policy recommendations to guide Nigeria’s AI future.

items.title: Explainable and Feature-Engineered Machine Learning for Stock Market Forecasting: A Survey of Lexicon-Based, Statistical, and Sentiment-Driven Approaches
items.abstract: Forecasting the direction and magnitude of stock price movements remains one of the most persistently difficult problems in applied machine learning, owing to the noisy, non-stationary, and weak-form-efficient character of financial time series. This survey examines three recent studies that approach the problem through complementary lenses: an explainable Decision Tree that builds dynamic, industry-specific lexicons from financial news to classify next-day price-change magnitude [1]; a feature-engineering and portfolio-construction pipeline that derives new price-based predictors via Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA), and a proposed Statistical Average Method (SAM) before applying eight regression architectures, including Bi-LSTM [2]; and an LSTM-based trend classifier that fuses FinBERT-scored Twitter sentiment with price data to forecast North American and European bank-stock movements during the macroeconomically turbulent year of 2022 [3]. Beyond summarising each study's objectives, methodology, data, and results, this survey situates the three works within the broader and rapidly evolving literature on deep sequence models (LSTM, Bi-LSTM, GRU, and transformer architectures), sentiment analysis with pretrained financial language models such as FinBERT, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) in finance. A structured comparative analysis contrasts the three studies along ten dimensions, including data sources, feature engineering, model architecture, explainability, validation design, and reported performance, while explicitly cautioning against directly ranking studies whose prediction tasks and evaluation metrics are not commensurable. A cross-domain case study of an attention-based legislative-vote predictor is retained to examine whether a learned similarity mechanism could improve on the fixed similarity rules used throughout the finance literature reviewed here. The survey's contribution lies in bringing explainable lexicon-based methods, statistically engineered price features, and sentiment-driven deep learning together within a single comparative framework, and in using that synthesis to identify concrete, evidence-grounded gaps around auxiliary-signal fusion, the explainability of high-accuracy sequence models, and cross-market generalisation.

items.title: Explainable artificial intelligence of things integrated spatio-temporal feature modeling for traffic congestion framework on intelligent urban mobility system
items.abstract: Abstract Recent developments of Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) are transforming several sectors like Industry 4.0, smart cities, intelligent healthcare, and smart transportation. The AIoT can be employed in urban mobility to enable real-time monitoring and intelligent decision-making in the transportation sector. Traffic congestion classification is a significant aspect of Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS), as the rising urban population has contributed to severe congestion complexity that impacts air quality, road safety, and travel time. Accurate classification of congestion patterns improves traffic management and mitigates environmental impacts. Although precisely predicting congestion spread is still problematic, owing to the complex, non-linear, and dynamic nature of traffic patterns. As deep learning advances, efficient models are required to address the challenges in smart urban mobility systems. Therefore, this study presents a Deep Learning-Based Urban Mobility Intelligent System for Traffic Congestion Framework (DLUMIS-TCF). The proposed DLUMIS-TCF model analyzes urban mobility data with trip-level records for precise traffic congestion level classification. The preprocessing stage includes missing value handling, outlier detection, feature scaling, temporal attribute extraction, and spatial coordinate utilization to prepare the data for effective learning. For feature selection, the model utilizes Elastic Net to select the relevant spatio-temporal features from the dataset. In addition, the traffic congestion level classification is performed using a heterogeneous spatiotemporal graph attention network. Furthermore, the optimization of the model is carried out using the AdaBelief optimizer to improve convergence and performance. To improve the interpretability of the model, SHAP is used to explain the contribution of input features toward the classification results. To assess the performance of the proposed DLUMIS-TCF model, experiments are carried out on an Urban Mobility Intelligence Dataset obtained from the Kaggle repository. The experimental results show the effectiveness of the proposed model in predicting traffic congestion compared to other methods. Thus, the proposed DLUMIS-TCF approach can be useful for urban traffic management, congestion control, and intelligent transportation systems.

items.title: Explainable Multimodal Artificial Intelligence for Precision Laboratory Diagnosis: Integrating Biomarkers, Molecular Profiles, Immunological Signatures, and Clinical Data
items.abstract: Background: Precision laboratory diagnosis increasingly relies on the interpretation of heterogeneous biological and clinical information. Conventional workflows tend to examine biomarkers, molecular measurements, immunological findings, and clinical characteristics along partly separate analytical pathways. Artificial intelligence (AI) can uncover complex relationships in high-dimensional biomedical data, yet many such systems remain hard to interpret at the point of clinical use. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) renders algorithmic outputs more transparent by identifying the features, modalities, and interactions that shape a prediction. Objective: This manuscript proposes an explainable multimodal AI framework for precision laboratory diagnosis, termed XMAI-PLD, which unites conventional laboratory biomarkers, molecular profiles, immunological signatures, and clinical data within a single analytical architecture. The framework is designed to support, rather than supplant, laboratory expertise and clinical judgement. Framework: The architecture comprises seven interconnected layers: data acquisition; quality control and harmonisation; modality-specific representation; multimodal fusion; diagnostic inference; explainability and uncertainty assessment; and laboratory–clinical decision support. Biomarker measurements contribute quantitative biochemical information, molecular profiles characterise genomic or molecular alterations, immunological signatures capture host-response patterns, and clinical variables supply patient-level context. Each stream is processed separately before being integrated through multimodal learning, and explanations are generated at the modality and feature levels to reveal the principal drivers of each output. Clinical and Laboratory Relevance: The framework addresses the shortcomings of isolated single-modality models, namely incomplete biological representation, heterogeneous data structures, missing information, analytical variability, and limited interpretability. Its proposed outputs comprise diagnostic probabilities, contributing features, modality-level evidence, uncertainty estimates, and cases flagged for human review. Particular emphasis falls on analytical validity, calibration, external validation, data provenance, subgroup assessment, cybersecurity, privacy, and human oversight. Conclusion: Explainable multimodal AI offers a promising route towards a more integrated diagnostic representation of laboratory and clinical evidence. Its worth will hinge not only on predictive performance but also on analytical robustness, reproducibility, interpretability, calibration, clinical usefulness, and sustained human oversight. Prospective, multicentre evaluation is required before such systems enter routine diagnostic practice.

items.title: Explaining FOMO Symptoms Based on Maladaptive Perfectionism and Emotional Loneliness with Emphasis on the Mediating Role of Artificial Intelligence Dependency among Female High School Adolescents
items.abstract: Objective: The present study aimed to explain FOMO (Fear of Missing Out) symptoms based on maladaptive perfectionism and emotional loneliness, with a particular focus on the mediating role of artificial intelligence dependency among female high school adolescents. Methods and Materials: This correlational study employed a structural equation modeling approach to investigate the relationships among maladaptive perfectionism, emotional loneliness, artificial intelligence dependency, and FOMO symptoms. The statistical population consisted of all female students enrolled in secondary high schools in Dezful, Iran, during the 2025–2026 academic year. A total of 250 students were selected through convenience sampling. Data were collected using the Fear of Missing Out Scale developed by Przybylski et al. (2013), the Multidimensional Perfectionism Questionnaire by Hewitt and Flett (2004), the Social and Emotional Loneliness Scale by DiTommaso et al. (2004), and the Artificial Intelligence Dependency Questionnaire developed by Huang et al. (2024). Data analysis was conducted using descriptive and inferential statistics in SPSS and AMOS software packages. Path analysis and structural equation modeling were utilized to evaluate both direct and indirect relationships among the study variables and to assess the overall model fit. Findings: The results demonstrated that maladaptive perfectionism and emotional loneliness significantly predicted FOMO symptoms both directly and indirectly through artificial intelligence dependency. Maladaptive perfectionism showed a significant positive effect on artificial intelligence dependency (β = 0.411, p < .01), while emotional loneliness also exhibited a significant positive effect on artificial intelligence dependency (β = 0.506, p < .01). Furthermore, maladaptive perfectionism had a significant direct effect on FOMO symptoms (β = 0.267, p < .01) and a significant indirect effect through artificial intelligence dependency (β = 0.124, p < .01). Similarly, emotional loneliness exerted a significant direct effect on FOMO symptoms (β = 0.259, p < .01) and a significant indirect effect mediated by artificial intelligence dependency (β = 0.152, p < .01). Artificial intelligence dependency itself significantly and positively predicted FOMO symptoms (β = 0.301, p < .01). Model fit indices indicated a satisfactory fit of the proposed structural model to the observed data. Conclusion: The findings suggest that adolescents with higher levels of maladaptive perfectionism and emotional loneliness are more likely to develop dependency on artificial intelligence technologies, which in turn intensifies FOMO symptoms. Artificial intelligence dependency functions as a significant psychological mechanism linking individual vulnerabilities and social-emotional difficulties to heightened fear of missing out. These results highlight the importance of addressing maladaptive perfectionistic standards, strengthening real-world emotional relationships, and promoting healthy patterns of AI use in interventions designed to reduce FOMO among adolescents.

items.title: Exploring Jailbreak Vulnerability Across Depth-Based Dynamic Inference in Large Language Models
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been shown to be computationally expensive and vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, in which adversarial prompts bypass safety alignment and induce harmful responses. To address this inefficiency, a range of techniques have been proposed to enable efficient LLM inference. Depth-based dynamic inference has demonstrated promising results by enabling outputs to be generated from intermediate layers. It offers the flexibility to adjust model behavior based on the available resource budget. However, how this flexibility affects the robustness of LLMs against jailbreak attacks remains unexplored. In this paper, we address this gap via a comprehensive investigation into the impact of depth-based dynamic inference on the robustness of LLMs against jailbreak attacks. Specifically, we make the following key observations: 1) Shallow exits are consistently more robust to jailbreak attacks than deeper ones; 2) Exit depth affects how easily the adversarial suffix can be optimized, with deeper exits reaching lower attack loss; and 3) Adversarial suffixes affect utility uniformly across exit depths. These insights can help design dynamic inference methodologies that are more robust to jailbreak attacks. Code is available at https://github.com/LassNajmuldeen/balcony-jailbreaking

items.title: Exploring rehabilitation therapists’ knowledge and perspectives on the use of artificial intelligence and machine learning for persons post-stroke
items.abstract: BackgroundThe integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) within the clinical work of rehabilitation therapists in post stroke rehabilitation has the potential to transform their work performance, habits, and routines. The impact could potentially enhance integration of assessment/data analysis, personalizing therapies, documentation, and promoting home program adherence.ObjectiveThis study assesses occupational and physical therapists' current perspectives on AI/ML in post-stroke clinical rehabilitation and examines perceived barriers to potential application of AI/ML in their clinical work.MethodsThis mixed methods study includes quantitative survey data collected pre/post an AI/ML educational webinar, as well as qualitative focus group analysis that includes therapist attitudes and experiences with AI/ML, practical applications to using AI/ML, as well as the difficulties associated. The recruited therapists include occupational and physical therapy practitioners from the United States and Asia. Individuals included in the study had to have a caseload of 30% persons with stroke.ResultsFour key themes emerged from qualitative analysis: 1) current clinical work practice and identified gaps, 2) current therapists' perceptions of AI/ML, 3) perceived future of AI/ML in clinical work practices and 4) steps needed for implementation. Survey data reporting frequencies of technology use and AI/ML perceptions are integrated into qualitative findings.ConclusionsTherapists can articulate potential future uses for AI/ML technology in post-stroke rehabilitation, however, remain uncertain about when, how, and at what cost utilization will be supported in clinical work environments. Therapists desire education and support to utilize the evolving technologies in practice.

items.title: Exposing AI Inference as a Telco Network API over the 5G User Plane
items.abstract: Supporting edge Artificial Intelligence (AI) inference as a network service is challenging because current mobile systems can transport tensors but do not expose or understand the inference context that gives those tensors operational meaning. Prior studies have addressed this gap through dynamic partitioning, collaborative inference, and split pipelines; however, these solutions remain application-bound, network-blind, or context-free. This work proposes Inference on Demand (IoD), an inference-on-demand abstraction that exposes split inference through a CAMARA-like Application Program Interface (API) and carries a split-aware tensor context in-band across the 5G user plane path. We evaluate the IoD on a programmable user plane function (UPF)-based testbed using a partitionable visual AI workload, showing that adaptive split selection can operate as a network-facing service while avoiding the rigid cost profile of static configurations. Including our findings, split inference becomes more than offloading when the service intent, runtime partitioning, and tensor transport are made visible to the mobile data plane. This opens a path toward network-native AI services, in which programmable telco infrastructure coordinates computation, context, and connectivity for user-facing applications.

items.title: FidelityQ: Preserving Predictive Fidelity in Ultra-Low-Bit Language Model Quantization
items.abstract: Ultra-low-bit scalar quantization offers a regular arithmetic structure for efficient deployment of large language models, but preserving predictive behavior at extreme precision remains challenging: with only a few reconstruction levels, accurate weight representation must translate into consistent predictions from a small calibration set. We propose FidelityQ, a scalar quantization framework that preserves predictive fidelity at weight precisions down to 2 bits. For accurate quantization, we introduce Information-Aligned Analytic Coding (IAC), which shapes each weight row toward a centered symmetric source via randomized Hadamard mixing and fits a mirrored four-level minimum-distortion quantizer to its empirical weights. Every level set in this family decomposes exactly into two sign-valued bases with associated scales, combining source-adaptive reconstruction with lookup-free decoding compatible with scaled integer arithmetic. Our analysis further shows that residual predictive discrepancies are heavy-tailed and concentrate on tokens the teacher predicts confidently, motivating Knowledge-Intensive Calibration (KIC) for consistent quantization. KIC ranks sequences by the tail of token-wise teacher-student divergence, allocates a limited calibration budget to the highest-scoring samples, and restores predictive agreement by updating only quantization levels and scales under teacher supervision, keeping pretrained weights frozen. Experiments on the LLaMA and Qwen families demonstrate the effectiveness of FidelityQ in weight-only and joint quantization settings. On LLaMA-2-7B, FidelityQ achieves a WikiText2 perplexity of 6.62 at W2A16 and improves the prior state-of-the-art W2A4KV4 result from 8.31 to 6.96, while reducing linear-layer weight memory by 8.0x relative to FP16.

items.title: FleetPilot: Fine-Grained Steering Empowers Real-World LLM Personalization
items.abstract: With the rapid evolution of large language models (LLMs), there is an increasing demand for effective personalization techniques that can adapt model behavior to individual user preferences. Personalized LLMs must infer a user's query-dependent preferences from limited, heterogeneous, and evolving interaction histories. Existing approaches rely primarily on in-context personalization, parametric adaptation, or personalized reward modeling, but respectively incur recurring costs in context management, model optimization and deployment, or multi-candidate generation and scoring. These limitations become particularly restrictive when user observations are sparse and the preference evidence relevant to each query varies across contexts and over time. To address these challenges, we propose \modelname, a fine-grained and instance-tailored steering framework that dynamically generates sample-level interference vectors from user data and injects them into the model's forward pass for personalized adaptation. Our approach introduces: match contrast that produces user-relevant signals, fine-grained steering component that captures nuanced signals by hooking activations from attention and MLP layers, and query-conditioned aggregation module that synthesizes these signals into contextually relevant enhancements. Extensive experiments across diverse scenarios, including short-to-long text generation, and web function calling, validate the effectiveness and compatibility of \modelname. Results show that our method consistently brings significant performance gains, and show extreme superiority in fast-shifting and data-sparse environments. Additionally, \modelname rids us of training cycles and incurs light overhead of storage or inference latency. These make \modelname a strong and real-world deployable method. Implementation is available \footnote{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/FleetPilot}.

items.title: From cyberspeak to algorithmic newspeak: soft derogation and the ethics of AI-generated language
items.abstract: Purpose This paper examines the ethical and epistemological implications of language generated by large language models (LLMs) through the lenses of speech act theory, conversational implicature and second-order cybernetics. LLMs are often presented as neutral tools, yet their outputs actively participate in shaping discourse in ways that carry consequences for meaning, responsibility and pluralism. Design/methodology/approach The paper introduces the concept of soft derogation to describe a form of linguistic exclusion, one that operates through euphemization, omission and the simulation of neutrality rather than overt offense. Such processes can subtly promote or suppress certain ideas, values or identities without transparent authorship or intention. The result is a shift toward an algorithmically generated form of newspeak, where expressive possibilities are narrowed through alignment protocols and safety layers. Findings Drawing on second-order cybernetics, the paper argues that ethical responsibility for AI-generated language is distributed across developers, deployers, institutional stakeholders and human interpreters. While users co-construct meaning within recursive socio-technical systems, the upstream actors who design alignment protocols, moderation layers and deployment conditions bear primary responsibility for the communicative environments they create. Originality/value Relatively little work has examined how the pertinent philosophical frameworks can illuminate forms of linguistic influence that operate through euphemization, omission and simulated neutrality. This paper addresses that gap by analyzing how algorithmically generated language can shape discourse while appearing neutral.

items.title: From Detection to Investigation: A Survey of Foundation Models and Agents for Financial Fraud and Financial Crime
items.abstract: Foundation models are extending research on financial fraud and financial crime from isolated risk detection to document understanding, relational analysis, and investigative workflows. A gap nevertheless separates model outputs from candidate evidence and actionable conclusions. This survey examines advances in six families of foundation models: language, vision, speech, temporal, graph, and tabular models. It compares their roles and limitations along two dimensions: the risk-control lifecycle and the directness of the supporting evidence. Existing studies show that pretraining can support representation reuse and the processing of unstructured information, with direct validation in some financial tasks. Cross-modal identity binding, information availability over time, report faithfulness, and case-level benefits require separate evaluation. Evidence on investigative agents spans prototypes, controlled tasks, expert assessments, and industry disclosures, which establish different aspects of workflow feasibility, task performance, and user assessment. Establishing gains in investigative efficiency and reductions in financial losses requires case-level comparative evidence. We examine entity and temporal alignment, the organization of candidate evidence, constrained tool execution, and investigative benchmark design, together with the implications of adversarial threats, privacy, fairness, and model risk governance. Research priorities should shift from expanding system functionality toward factual traceability, sufficient evidence for decisions, and reviewable actions.

items.title: From revision to learning transfer: Self- and socially shared-regulated pathways in AI-assisted feedback
items.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has transformed feedback provision in writing practices. However, little is known about the mechanisms through which AI-mediated engagement and revision contribute to longer-term learning transfer. Research aims Framed by theories of self-regulated learning (SRL), socially shared regulated learning (SSRL), and cognitive engagement, the study examined the relationship among engagement, immediate revision gains, and longer-term learning transfer in AI-assisted feedback. Methods This 16-week cluster-randomized experiment involving 108 undergraduates in China compared two feedback modes: AI-assisted self-feedback and AI-assisted peer feedback. Analyses drew on 1100 writing samples (including pretests, four assignments with two drafts each, and posttests), and 432 reflection forms on AI feedback. Findings Linear mixed models revealed a decoupling of learning and performance: while both conditions produced similarly strong second drafts, AI-assisted peer feedback demonstrated significantly greater learning transfer to subsequent tasks. In AI-assisted self-feedback, learning followed a performance-dependent SRL cycle in which AI engagement and revision improvements independently predicted learning. A threshold-like pattern further showed that benefits emerged only when students engaged constructively, measured by reflection forms, to internalize writing standards. Conversely, AI-assisted peer feedback was associated with stronger learning transfer that was less dependent on revision gains or engagement with AI, a pattern consistent with an SSRL perspective emphasizing interactive engagement and co-constructed understanding. Conclusion These findings highlight the importance of revision mechanisms and depth of engagement across feedback contexts. The study contributes to theories of regulation and cognitive engagement and offers pedagogical and design implications for fostering meaningful learning through AI-assisted feedback.
